Spain landed a second star after finally beating a black hole of an Argentina team in the World Cup final.

Lionel Messi may not have got the ending that much of the world at one point wanted but few can say the winners weren’t the right champions for the World Cup 2026 final.

Spain have been the best team and they were duly the only team actually playing to win this otherwise dismal occasion across more than 120 minutes.

It had an argument to be the worst final of all - which subsequently descended into chaos after Leandro Paredes’ antics in the final whistle - other than Ferran Torres rising above it all to send the ball high into the Argentina net.

His superbly-taken 106th minute goal ensures he is now part of World Cup lore alongside Andres Iniesta.

Enzo Fernandez meanwhile enters infamy, as he becomes the sixth player to be sent off in the final. Three of them are Argentine and it really could have been more here, with Paredes given his punishment after the final whistle.

The two others came in 1990 and this game had so many echoes of that, right down to a tired and stale side with a fading legend ultimately falling late on.

Argentina became the first finalists to complete the 90 minutes without recording a shot. Defeat was fully deserved.

Messi, in probably his last World Cup game, could barely get a touch until the climax. Then again, Lamine Yamal didn’t do much either, outside one fine free-kick towards the end.

Some of that was admittedly down to aggressive Argentine double-making, as the 23rd final almost immediately entered a defined and distinctive pattern.

Spain had all of the ball, and Argentina did almost nothing except defend deep.

The beaten finalists were only enlivened by Torres’s goal, which at last saw Messi come alive.

open image in gallery Spain's Ferran Torres lifts the trophy with teammates ( Reuters )

open image in gallery Spain players celebrate after winning the World Cup ( Reuters )

open image in gallery Spain celebrate winning the World Cup ( Getty )

It was all too brief, in too limited time.

Argentina might have tried to do more… but they wouldn’t, or maybe couldn’t.

It is probably the deposed champions who will provoke more debate and discussion from this game, but Spain do deserve immense credit.

That went beyond actually trying to play in this final, and rising above this World Cup of individual stars by actually playing as a team.

Luis de la Fuente again turned a game with his subs, and there was a symbolism in another squad player - the impact attacker Torres - who entered history. This is a proper collective, a team that play with an idea.

That ensured they actually had multiple chances to win this before the end.

It looked like it might be one of those days - on the worst day of all - as Mikel Merino missed a header right in front of goal and Nico Williams had a goal controversially disallowed.

It just wasn’t happening.

open image in gallery Spain's Ferran Torres celebrates scoring their first goal ( Reuters )

open image in gallery Spain's Ferran Torres celebrates scoring their first goal with Nico Williams ( Reuters )

And from that, there would have been almost deliciously grim football perverseness had Argentina managed it from there.

This was the most expensive match of all time after the highest-grossing World Cup, too, with the financial obsession reflected in the number of celebrities Fifa were proudly publicising as attending. There was even the anti-football farce of a half-time show, as the notional global safeguards of the game usher in another new precedent that football’s actual community have long been resisting.

That display - especially some real mood-killing songs - was still somehow worse than a turgid first half, and raised quite a prospect.

All of these celebrities there, Fifa all too willing to cut to them on the big screen, and here they were grimly sitting through an anti-football team turgidly grinding it out to a potential penalty shoot-out win. Maybe it's what Fifa deserved, too, after Gianni Infantino and Donald Trump were booed.

That’s football.

Except, this wasn’t really football. It would have been too bad, a level beyond.

open image in gallery Argentina's Lionel Messi and Rodrigo De Paul look dejected ( Reuters )

open image in gallery Lionel Messi #10 of Argentina receives his runner-up medal from U.S. President Donald Trump ( Getty )

Argentina have surely put in the most miserable display ever seen in this fixture, and that’s including teams who lost 4-2 and 5-2.

They at least tried to play.

And sure, maybe some allowances can be made. Argentina were probably exhausted after Wednesday. This trend continues of the first semi-finalist winning the final, with the only team breaking it in modern history the Spanish themselves in 2010.

They’re probably exactly the wrong team you want to play in those circumstances. They just keep the ball away from you until you become exhausted.

It’s almost a matter of maths, Spain creating all of the angles and shutting off most of the openings until eventually there’s a break.

Except, they were also in their own race against time.

open image in gallery ( AP Photo/Abbie Parr )

open image in gallery ( Reuters )

But this was worse than just defending from Argentina. There was a clear intimidation to their play, a gamesmanship perhaps taken to inevitable extremes, and aided by a permissive referee.

He let a lot go, until he eventually had no choice but to send off Fernandez.

It was all so different to the last World Cup, right up to the feeling around Argentina and Messi.

No one can surely think it’s a shame he doesn’t ultimately win it here. Not after that and what his teammates did.

And, after that, there is potentially new reflection for England too, as they now become the only country to have won the World Cup only once.

How did they lose to this team, given Spain finally exposed them? It only emphasises the tactics were wrong in that semi-final.

open image in gallery Argentina's Lionel Messi looks dejected as Spain players celebrate winning ( PA )

open image in gallery Lamine Yamal #19 of Spain celebrates with teammates ( Getty )

It had long been felt that Argentina had so many flaws they would eventually lose to the first elite team they played and this was that - even if it took much longer than anticipated.

Of course, the reflection for England should actually be far deeper.

It should really be how you evolve an idea like in the way Spain do.

It doesn’t even need to be the same, since no one can play this to the depth Spain can and not everyone would even want to.

But merely having that football lesson is an amplification of all their talents, ensuring they have been by some distance the best team.

And now, very deservedly, world champions for the second time.

Not just a victory on the greatest stage of all, but a lesson, and a moral victory.

Vice President JD Vance and Second Lady Usha Vance announced the birth of their fourth child on Sunday.

Alec Neel Vance was born this morning.

“Usha and the baby are happy and healthy, and our kids are overjoyed to meet their little brother,” the Vances wrote in a statement on X.

“The incredible military doctors and staff members of Walter Reed Medical Center and the White House Medical Unit have been a blessing,” the statement added. “We are deeply thankful for all they have done for our family.”

The second lady announced she was pregnant in January.

Vice President JD Vance and Second Lady Usha Vance announced that their fourth child, Alec, was born on Sunday ( Getty )

The couple share three other children: Ewan, 9; Vivek, 6; and Mirabel, 4.

Vice President Vance said on a podcast in June that he and the second lady had been having “an ongoing conversation for a couple of years” about having a fourth child, given the difficulty of being in the spotlight and the challenges on Usha Vance of having a baby at age 40.

“I remember when we decided to run for vice president, I said, ‘Honey, I really want to have a fourth kid.’ And she said, ‘Well, you can become vice president or you can have a fourth baby,’” Vance said at a White House event in March. “But, ladies and gentlemen, I am persuasive, because I got both.”

This is a breaking news story and will be updated with new information.

Tropical Storm Fausto formed Sunday well off Mexico's southwest Pacific coast, while a tropical depression meandering in warm Gulf of Mexico waters south of the Florida Panhandle was threatening to strengthen into a named storm.

Fausto emerged from a tropical depression about 750 miles (1,200 kilometers) south-southwest of the southern tip of Mexico’s Baja California peninsula and was expected to undergo steady or rapid strengthening and become a hurricane by Monday night, the U.S. National Hurricane Center said.

The storm had maximum sustained winds of 40 mph (65 kph) and was moving to the west-northwest at 13 mph (20 kph). No coastal watches or warnings were in effect.

Also in the eastern Pacific, Tropical Storm Elida was weakening Sunday and expected to become a remnant low within a couple of days. Elida was centered Sunday about 1,015 miles (1,635 kilometers) west of the southern Baja peninsula and had top sustained winds of 60 mph (95 kph).

Meanwhile, forecasters at the Miami-based hurricane center said they were closely watching the evolution of a tropical depression fueled by warm waters south-southeast of the Florida Panhandle.

Forecasters said the depression was expected to strengthen into a tropical storm early in the week. A tropical storm watch was issued for parts of the Florida Panhandle to the Alabama border. The slow-moving storm is expected to move near or along the northern Gulf Coast during the next several days.

The system could bring heavy rainfall to coastal areas of northern Florida, Alabama and Louisiana as it eventually churns west toward Texas, the hurricane center said.

On Sunday afternoon, the depression was virtually stationary and located about 190 miles (310 kilometers) south-southeast of Panama City, Florida, with top sustained winds of 30 mph (45 kph).

A father has praised the medical staff who cared for his teenage son during brain tumour surgery, which utilised innovative 3D exoscope technology.

This advanced system, designed to enhance precision and improve outcomes in complex neurological procedures, has been introduced at the Royal Hospital for Children in Glasgow.

NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde confirmed it is the first in Scotland to install the B Braun Aesculap Aeos 3D Robotic Assisted Exoscope.

The technology provides "exceptional" image quality, powerful illumination, and enhanced depth perception, offering surgeons a clearer view.

Thirteen-year-old Toby Peart, from Strathpeffer in the Highlands, was one of the first patients to undergo surgery using the new system. His symptoms, including pins and needles and pain in his left leg, began in April 2025 and progressively worsened over several months.

open image in gallery Toby Peart on a stand-up paddle board ( PA )

He had an MRI scan at Raigmore Hospital in Inverness which found he had a brain tumour, and within days he was referred to the Glasgow facility for specialist treatment.

An operation was recommended after further investigations confirmed a tumour measuring about 13–14mm on the right side of his brain, which proved to be non-cancerous, and he underwent surgery in November 2025.

His father Marc said: “It was without question the hardest few weeks of our lives. Toby is a quiet, gentle boy who never complains, so when he told us he was in pain, we knew something wasn’t right.

“Everything happened incredibly quickly. One day we were expecting to wait a couple of weeks for MRI results and the next we were being told that Toby had a brain tumour and needed specialist treatment in Glasgow. It was a huge shock for all of us.”

He and his wife Adie were advised by the surgical teams that post-surgery outcomes could include loss of sight or paralysis.

When Toby woke from surgery, he initially experienced weakness and paralysis on his left side, but he went on to make rapid progress during his recovery with support from a multidisciplinary team.

Mr Peart said: “When Toby came out of surgery, he couldn’t move his left arm or leg and couldn’t feel anything. At that point, we didn’t know whether that would be permanent or whether things would improve.

“A few days later, I woke up and saw him using his right hand to lift his left hand into the air. He looked at me and said, ‘Dad, quick, look, my fingers are doing finger things.’ It was one of the most remarkable moments of my life.

open image in gallery The surgical team with the 3D exoscope at the Royal Hospital for Children in Glasgow ( NHSGGC/PA Wire )

“Every day he got a little stronger. The care he received was incredible and it was amazing to watch his determination.

“Just a week after surgery, we were told he was ready to go home. Walking out of the hospital with Toby was an emotional moment and one we’ll never forget. We’re so grateful to (neurosurgeon) Mr O’Kane and the entire team who cared for him.

“We know not every family’s journey is the same, but we feel incredibly fortunate. Toby was back at school in January and he’s doing really well.”

The technology has also been designed with the wellbeing of surgeons in mind and enables them to work in a more upright posture as it features a “heads-up” 3D display, unlike traditional microscopes that require prolonged “head-down” positioning.

Roddy O’Kane, consultant neurosurgeon at NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde, said: “Traditionally, neurosurgery meant working for hours with your eyes fixed to microscope eyepieces.

“This technology allows us to operate upright while gaining views and angles that simply aren’t possible with conventional microscopes.

open image in gallery The 3D exoscope at the hospital ( NHSGGC/PA Wire )

“For children undergoing brain surgery, that enhanced visualisation can make a real difference.

“The ability to see more clearly and reach more effectively supports safer surgery and, ultimately, better outcomes.”

Emer Campbell, clinical lead and consultant neurosurgeon at the health board, said: “We’re delighted to have this technology in place.

“Beyond the clear benefits for our patients, we’re already seeing how it enhances teamwork, workflow and training in theatre.”

The average asking price for a home entering the market in July saw a notable dip, falling by £3,832 month-on-month, according to property website Rightmove.

This 1.0 per cent decrease significantly outpaced the typical July decline of 0.2 per cent observed over the past decade.

Across Britain, the average asking price now stands at £372,359.

Rightmove attributes this slowdown to a combination of factors, including the World Cup and unusually hot weather, which, alongside traditional summer holiday distractions, have diverted potential buyers' attention.

Sellers are reportedly facing increased competition to attract these distracted summer buyers in a market characterised by high supply.

open image in gallery The 1.0 per cent decrease significantly outpaced the typical July decline of 0.2 per cent observed over the past decade. ( Reuters )

While the number of available homes for sale is marginally down by 1 per cent compared to last year, it remains remarkably close to a 12-year high for this period, further intensifying the competitive landscape for those looking to sell.

Rightmove said that May’s hot weather coincided with a temporary fall in buyer demand before rebounding, and similar dips in demand coincided with the hot weather in June and July.

Colleen Babcock, a property expert at Rightmove, said: “This month’s larger-than-normal price fall reflects the reality of a market where buyers have plenty of choice and sellers are having to work harder to stand out and attract them.

“They’re also competing with an unusual number of distractions which have been keeping the minds of some potential buyers occupied, namely the World Cup and the hot weather.

“While these diversions are short term, they’re adding to what is already a distracting summer holiday period to create a challenging selling environment.”

Rightmove said the first six months of 2026 have presented challenges for home movers, with mortgage rates having jumped amid the conflict in the Middle East.

Highlighting the importance to sellers of getting their prices right from the outset, Rightmove said that nearly three-quarters (74%) of homes selling and completing this year did so without an asking price reduction.

Homes that do require an asking price reduction spend an average of 127 days on the market, compared with just 36 days for those that sell without a reduction, the website said.

Ms Babcock added: “Pricing remains critical, and it’s remarkable that nearly three-quarters of homes that have sold so far this year have done so without needing an asking price reduction.”

Matt Smith, a mortgage expert at Rightmove, said: “Mortgage rates are higher than many buyers would have hoped for at the start of the year, and the increases due to the war in Iran have understandably dented confidence for some.

“However, lenders remain keen to lend, and the mortgage market is still competitive.”

Chris Thomas, managing director at Wiglesworth & Co Estate Agents in Leamington Spa, Warwickshire, said: “In the type of market we’re in currently, there are some clear rules that sellers need to follow to successfully find a buyer.

“Firstly, accuracy of pricing is everything and getting the price right the first time gives sellers the best chance.

“Secondly, sellers need to choose an agent who knows the local area and market extremely well and has a proven strong track record of giving honest and professional advice.

“There are still buyers active in the market and positive signs that mortgage rates could be easing.”

Nathan Emerson, CEO of property professionals’ body Propertymark, said: “While the year initially started with optimism in the housing market, global unease has in many ways dominated the agenda ever since.

“Rightly so, many consumers have been exercising greater caution with their spending to help ensure household budgets are better protected against unforeseen increases in expenditure.”

The widening pay gap between chief executives of leading companies and their workers is the widest in eight years, new research has revealed.

The High Pay Centre reported that the median pay ratio for FTSE 100 chief executives and workers was 130:1 , an increase from 124:1 last year.

This comes as median FTSE 100 CEO pay reached a record £5.06 million, marking an 8.6 per cent rise from £4.66 million in 2024/25, the think tank added. FTSE 100 firms collectively spent over £850 million on executive remuneration in the past year, the report also noted.

The High Pay Centre said excessive spending on top earners by leading firms often comes at the expense of pay increases for the rest of the workforce, and called for reforms to regulations affecting the corporate pay-setting process.

open image in gallery The FTSE 100 ( PA Archive )

High Pay Centre interim director Andrew Speke said: “The substantial growth in the gap between executive and worker pay in the past year should be a wake-up call to those who’ve turned a blind eye to rising executive pay.

“As our findings show, this is the fourth year in a row that FTSE 100 executive pay has risen, and this growth is starting to substantially outstrip growth in worker pay.

“We hope that a change in prime minister and a renewed focus on economic fairness will lead to economic inequality and corporate excess returning up the political agenda.

“A failure to tackle such disproportionate and inefficient levels of inequality will only further reduce faith in our current economic model and help to accelerate the rise of right-wing populism.”

Last week, new research suggested an increasing number of adults are worried about employment as the labour market continues to slow down.

The Work Foundation said that as concerns about employment rise, its study found that one in eight employers have made redundancies in the last year and real wages have started to stagnate.

Aman Navani, senior researcher at the think tank, said: “The new prime minister arrives in office at a time when an increasing number of people are worried about the future of employment in the UK.

“One in two UK adults are worried about employment, which has risen by 13 percentage points on the year.”

Andy Burnham's ambition to transform Britain's housing market are under threat as the housebuilding industry faces its toughest conditions since the financial crisis, with developers grappling with rising costs, weakening demand and higher borrowing costs.

The new prime minister has argued that a radical expansion of social and affordable housing is essential to tackling the chronic housing shortage, and has repeatedly called for greater public investment and powers to build at scale.

But the economic backdrop confronting ministers and developers suggests delivering those ambitions will be far from easy.

The latest figures paint a sobering picture. England saw 208,600 new homes built in 2024/25, a 6 per cent fall on the previous year and the lowest annual total since 2015/16, highlighting the scale of the challenge facing Labour's pledge to deliver 1.5 million homes during this Parliament.

While Homes England reported more than 40,000 homes were completed through its own programmes in 2025/26 – four in five of them affordable homes – broader housing supply remains well below the pace needed to meet the government's targets. Since Labour entered government in July 2024, around 392,400 net additional homes have been delivered, leaving ministers running at roughly two-thirds of the rate required to hit their goal by 2029.

open image in gallery Housebuilding firms are already warning of a hit to profits (Gareth Fuller/PA) ( PA Wire )

The pressure is being compounded by a deteriorating commercial outlook for housebuilders, amid higher mortgage costs and lingering uncertainty over interest rates.

Housebuilders’ strife

Britain's biggest listed housebuilders are issuing profit warnings at a rate not seen since the global financial crisis, underlining the severity of the downturn gripping the sector.

According to EY-Parthenon, home construction companies issued eight profit warnings during the first half of 2026, matching the level recorded during the first half of 2008 and marking the highest total since the Covid pandemic.

Since 2020, UK-listed housebuilders have issued 47 profit warnings – almost double the number recorded during the previous 13 years combined.

The consultancy says developers are being squeezed by a combination of:

higher labour, materials and energy costs

tighter financing conditions

weaker consumer confidence

planning delays and regulatory complexity

persistent skills shortages

slowing demand across the wider housing market

Tim Vance, restructuring partner at EY-Parthenon, said many firms had entered 2026 expecting falling interest rates to revive demand, only to be hit by renewed economic uncertainty.

Developers have increasingly relied on incentives such as deposit contributions and mortgage support schemes to secure sales, but those incentives have further eroded already-thin profit margins.

The warnings are already translating into weaker financial results.

Crest Nicholson has just swung from a profit to a £35.2m pre-tax loss and cut its earnings outlook, citing weaker consumer confidence and slower housing market activity. Estate agent Foxtons has also warned that subdued demand is likely to leave profits millions of pounds below previous expectations.

open image in gallery Andy Burnham’s ambitious plans to boost social and affordable housing are under threat ( Getty Images )

Mortgages

Even if more homes are built, many prospective buyers face a very different affordability landscape from just a few years ago.

Mortgage rates remain significantly higher than those available during the ultra-low interest rate era, leaving households facing sharply higher repayments when fixed-rate deals expire.

More than one million homeowners are expected to remortgage this year, with many moving from fixed deals of around 2 per cent to rates above 5 per cent.

For some borrowers, monthly repayments are expected to double.

Mortgage adviser Lorna Hopes, of Smith and Pinching, says the impact extends well beyond first-time buyers.

“When households suddenly find hundreds of pounds more each month going towards their mortgage, they tend not to move home. They stay put, spend less elsewhere and that slows activity across the wider housing market.”

The effect is particularly acute for buyers who purchased their first property five years ago and still require high loan-to-value mortgages, limiting access to the cheapest deals.

Meanwhile, average mortgage pricing remains elevated. Moneyfacts data this week showed average two-year and five-year fixed homeowner mortgage rates hovering at around 5.5 per cent, despite some lenders making modest reductions in recent weeks.

Interest rates

The Bank of England has eased monetary policy from its recent peak, but borrowing costs remain well above the levels that fuelled the housing boom of the late 2010s.

Earlier hopes that interest rates would fall rapidly this year have faded following renewed geopolitical tensions and stubborn inflationary pressures.

open image in gallery Stubborn interest rates are a barrier to those seeking mortgages ( PA )

Those expectations matter because housing transactions are driven as much by confidence as by affordability.

Higher mortgage pricing has weighed heavily on first-time buyers, who accounted for more than half of all purchase mortgages last year but are also the most sensitive to changes in borrowing costs because they typically borrow close to their maximum affordability.

Peter Stimson, director of mortgages at MPowered Mortgages, says first-time buyers remain “the key to the property market”, with knock-on effects across furniture, home improvements and the wider economy.

He believes mortgage rates could gradually ease if inflation remains under control and the Bank of England begins cutting rates again next year, potentially bringing more buyers back into the market.

But for now, many households continue to delay purchases.

Burnham's housing dream

Against that backdrop, Burnham's vision of dramatically increasing housebuilding faces formidable obstacles.

The new Labour leader has argued that Britain needs a new generation of social housing and has repeatedly called for greater powers and funding to accelerate development, particularly in his former patch of Greater Manchester.

His proposals are aimed at addressing a structural shortage that has developed over decades and improving affordability for younger households locked out of home ownership.

However, even if planning reforms succeed in unlocking more land, developers still face weaker demand, higher financing costs and squeezed profit margins that make new projects less attractive commercially.

The mismatch illustrates one of the biggest dilemmas facing Labour's housing agenda: political ambition alone cannot overcome economic headwinds.

Without stronger consumer confidence, lower mortgage costs and healthier balance sheets across the construction sector, delivering the scale of housebuilding needed to meet Labour's targets—and the wider ambitions championed by Burnham—will remain an uphill battle.

The danger for ministers is that Britain's housing shortage continues to worsen just as the industry needed to solve it enters one of its most difficult periods since the financial crash.

News.title: Spain v Argentina LIVE: Ugly scenes after full time as Spain win second World Cup in their history
News.content:
Spain lift World Cup 2026 trophy after defeating Argentina

Spain won the World Cup for the second time in their history as they claimed a 1-0 extra-time victory over 10-man Argentina before ugly scenes on the pitch after full time marred the celebrations.

Ferran Torres’ smashed finish in the 106th minute was enough for Spain to add to their 2010 triumph but Argentina – who offered little throughout the match – reacted badly after the final whistle, with players brawling, Leandro Paredes sent off after grabbing Eric Garcia by the throat and reports of punches being thrown.

Donald Trump then unsurprisingly inserted himself into things post-match as he lurked towards the edge of Spain’s trophy lift to ensure he was in the photo, despite Gianni Infantino trying to usher him away, after presenting the Spanish players with medals and the trophy. However, the US president was audibly booed when he first walked on to the pitch with Infantino.

After a dire spectacle for 90 minutes, with neither side mustering any real chances, Enzo Fernandez stupidly got himself sent off just before the end of normal time when he crunched Pau Cubarsi on halfway and was deservedly shown a second yellow card, having earlier been booked for dissent. Spain then finally made the breakthrough when Torres calmly hammered home at the start of the second half of extra time and it meant Lionel Messi was denied on surely his final World Cup appearance, with the aftermath further souring the occasion for the 39-year-old football icon.

Relive all the action from the World Cup final, below:

News.title: Hamilton takes out Russell as Antonelli stretches lead with Belgian GP win
News.content:
Welcome to our live coverage for the 2026 Belgian Grand Prix from Spa-Francorchamps. The story of yesterday and in fact the weekend was of everyone trying to dislodge Kimi Antonelli from the top of the timesheets. Spoiler alert if you did not watch qualifying: they failed.

That is not to say the fight wasn’t a half-decent one. Max Verstappen and Red Bull were the closest challengers in the end, demonstrating an element of revival during a tricky season. Whether that will continue during the race is hard to know. Verstappen certainly thought he would have been further down the field without the tremendous tow he received from Isack Hadjar, his Red Bull team-mate, in the final sector.

Lando Norris also pushed Verstappen, though was almost half a second down on Antonelli’s time in the end. Unfortunately he will not be able to take advantage of a start from third place because he takes a 10-place grid penalty. George Russell, who has managed to reduce his Mercedes team-mate’s advantage to just 25 points in the past few rounds, was fourth and will start third. He did however, have a difficult session once again, finishing more than half a second off his team-mate.

He was at a loss to explain this. Well, he knows where he lost most of the time: on the straights. But he still does not understand exactly why it is happening. The good news for him is that third place is often the most optimal starting position at this track.

Will that be the case today? Let’s see...

News.title: Ryan Fox matches father Grant’s sporting folklore with Claret Jug
News.content:
It’s the final day of the Open Championship, golf’s oldest and most-prestigious major. The leaderboard offers up hope of a seesaw day where little-known-of golfers tussle it out with big names under the north-west English sun. All in all, it should be an exciting day.

But, as with the past two days, we head into the round with talk dominated by a certain Bryson DeChambeau. It’s as frustrating and annoying as it is, in these days dominated by social media/content etc etc, painfully predictable. So let’s get the DeChambeau news out the way. Having been fairly hit with a two-shot penalty for improving his lie on Friday, the YouTube content creator had a tantrum, threatened to withdraw, caused a delay in the release of third-round tee times, before turning up and shooting a one-under 69 to lie four behind the leader heading into today.

That’s not all, The Bryson DeChambeau Show carried on after yesterday’s round where James Corrigan takes up the script...

Bryson DeChambeau marched straight to the offices of the R&A after being heckled with a cry of “you’re a cheat” on Birkdale’s 18th green on Saturday. As the controversy over his two-shot penalty from Friday’s second round rumbled on, Telegraph Sport understands DeChambeau, who shot a third-round 69 to lie four shots off the lead of the Open, asked R&A chief executive Mark Darbon for his scorecard from Friday. It is against policy so his request was rejected. DeChambeau then went back to the recorder’s hut and asked if they had it. Again, the answer was in the negative. It is unclear why he wanted it, but a theory emerged that he wished to put it on his social media channels.

All in all it is pathetic posturing that you’d expect from a stroppy teenager. He’s only three off the lead and has the game to win at Royal Birkdale, he’d do well to forget the perceived slights (whatever they may be) and get on with trying to win the Claret Jug.

Oh, and to add another scene to the soap opera Rory McIlroy doubtless spoke for many inside and outside the rope when he called out DeChambeau saying: “Yeah, look, I won’t pretend to be up here and defend Bryson. I’m not particularly fond of him. I think a lot of it’s performative. I think a lot of it’s for attention. To hold the tournament hostage like that, and to have all of us, players, volunteers, everyone waiting on him to depart, I didn’t feel like it was a great look.”

So, I think it’s best we focus on the golf today and not the theatrics and sorry antics of the American.

Sam Burns, his playing partner yesterday, was brilliant as he backed up his 62 of Friday with a five-under 65. He leads by two on 10 under and is the man to beat. Lurking behind with intent are a host of big names and big hitters – Ryan Fox (eight under), Si Woo Kim (eight under), Lucas Herbert (six under), Ludvig Aberg (seven under) and the man himself YouTube’s very own DeChambeau (six under).

Also in with a hint of a hope is Tommy Fleetwood, the hometown boy in search of his first major, the Englishman will start the round on five under.

Stay here for all the action, where I hope all the talk during and after the day’s round is focused on the winner’s brilliance rather than the emotions of DeChambeau.

News.title: Records tumble at Lord’s as England win thriller against India
News.content:
When he fell, bowled trying to sweep Bethell, India were 260 for two, still a tough ask but not impossible, especially against an England side with plenty of demons. Kohli fired up in Rohit’s absence, hitting Will Jacks for two sixes and Bethell into the pavilion.

But the run-rate faltered as Curran whipped out his slower-ball bag of tricks. He had Ishan Kishan and Shreyas Iyer caught in the deep by sub Rehan Ahmed in the 44th over and Kohli in the next, slapping a catch to cover. The rest subsided, India short in the end at 360 for seven.

England’s ODI side have struggled for runs under Brendon McCullum and this was easily their best batting performance, not just for the collection of records but for the calm, controlled way they went about setting a huge total. The openers Duckett and Bethell gave them a 192-run cushion, Root was impregnable again and Buttler finished it off, proving what he can do when others give him a platform. India were without Jasprit Bumrah but that should not take the shine off England’s achievements.

This was the first Duckett-Bethell opening contribution and it was England’s highest for the first wicket since the last World Cup. Jason Roy and Jonny Bairstow were such an important part of the route to World Cup glory and they left a huge hole in the side. Duckett and Bethell are more touch players, capable of gear shifts rather than setting out at turbo pace like Roy and Bairstow. The fact they bat so often together in Test cricket, where Bethell appears at No 3, helps the level of understanding.

Duckett’s innings knocked Viv Richards’s 138 in the 1979 World Cup final off the top spot at Lord’s and continued the form he showed at the end of the New Zealand Test series when he scored his first Test hundred in nearly a year. He was out first ball in the second ODI in Cardiff but was never in any real bother at Lord’s as he compiled a fourth century in this format.

News.title: England win gives Borthwick breathing space after late try controversy
News.content:
And in doing so he may have just saved Borthwick’s job.

The Rugby Football Union, following its review into England’s Six Nations campaign that yielded just one victory, had publicly offered its backing to its head coach through to the World Cup. But in reality, there are no guarantees. It needed evidence of England’s progress.

Two wins from three rounds of the Nations Championship is likely to convince RFU chief executive Bill Sweeney to back his man. But Borthwick will know that nothing can be taken for granted.

Four years ago, Eddie Jones, facing similar scrutiny from his employers, looked to have salvaged his job by winning the last two matches in a three-Test summer tour of Australia. But it did still not save him from the sack the following November.

Still. There was enough character and attacking prowess to convince the RFU that, despite the flaws in this display, the team are on the right track again.

It was still far from an 80-minute performance, but this was England’s first away victory in a year, in a hostile environment and after all the challenges, both physical and mental, the players have faced in travelling to three continents over three weeks – clocking up more than 25,000 miles – at the end of a long season.

England wobbled alarmingly earlier in the second half but remarkably found the resilience to drag themselves back into the game just as it looked like it was slipping from their grasp. That is clear evidence of players playing for their coach and each other.

Discipline, however, remains a major problem for Borthwick’s England. They had been cruising to what would looked to have been a statement victory at half-time following tries by Tommy Freeman and two by Ben Earl, in what had been their finest half of rugby this year.

And yet, once again indiscipline undermined their efforts. Remarkably, they were shown four yellow cards – Jack van Poortvliet, Alex Coles, Pollock (to more booing) and Emmanuel Iyogun – in the second half to take their total to 14 in their last 10 Tests, and at one stage were down to 12 men but, significantly, this time it did not prove fatal.

News.title: Tuchel learns lesson as England clinch third place in 10-goal thriller
News.content:
Neither England nor France wanted to be playing this game in Miami, but they can have no complaints about the nature of their semi-final defeats.

Tournament favourites France were comprehensively outplayed by Spain, with their feted front four of Kylian Mbappe, Ousmane Dembele, Bradley Barcola and Michael Olise all turning in below-par performances.

England’s defeat by Argentina was perhaps not as much of a surprise, but the nature of Thomas Tuchel’s team’s second-half collapse was just as alarming as France’s no-show.

England’s manager was fiercely criticised for replacing Anthony Gordon with Ezri Konsa and switching to a back five in the 72nd minute, but Tuchel has since defended his decisions.

“If you are asking if I regret my decisions, if this is the question, then I say no. I don’t regret my ‌decisions because I ‌felt that we became ⁠too passive,” said Tuchel.

“I took several decisions, trusting my instinct, my intuition, my experience, trusting my competitiveness, and I took the decision in order to help the team and get the result.

“I would regret if I didn’t help. I would regret ⁠if we didn’t react, but I have no regrets over the decision itself.”

Quite how strong Didier Deschamps and Tuchel decide to go with their teams is anyone’s guess. There has been some suggestion that Mbappe will start to give him the chance to beat Lionel Messi to the Golden Boot.

Some of England’s regular starters, such as Declan Rice, look physically spent, so there could be some rotation, and even a chance for players such as Kobbie Mainoo who has not played a minute of football at the tournament.

The third/fourth-place play-off has been rebranded as the “Bronze Final” for this tournament, and Tuchel was keen to point out that finishing third would be England’s best World Cup result since 1966. They lost this fixture against Belgium in 2018, but the way that game has been widely forgotten speaks volumes.

Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: Scotland fight back to claim victory against Fiji in Nations Championship
News.content:
A barrelling Schoeman finished an initial break by match captain Stafford McDowall, then Dobie burrowed over beside the posts in the 61st minute to put Scotland in front for the first time in 40 minutes.

Scotland glossed up the scoreline with two more tries in the last six minutes by Cummings and Dobie again to send home a crowd of 55,000 happy.

“I thought our bench did really well,” Townsend told the BBC. “Something I’ve learned over the last 12 months, the bench can help you change momentum. The players can come up with solutions themselves but the bench can give you energy and solutions but also bravery. We’re a team that will back our decisions and that put real pressure on Fiji.

“I felt [Fiji] picked their strongest side today and it took a lot of work for us to break them down but also it took a really good defensive performance,” Townsend added. “Fiji didn’t really break us that often [and] in that final quarter the guys were outstanding. We’ll take a few positives from that.”

Fiji had never beaten Scotland at Murrayfield but would have sensed the chance of making history by half-time. The Fijians were tough and clinical in a huge turnaround from last weekend when they were humiliated by England 73-8 in Liverpool.

News.title: Hometown hero Tommy Fleetwood facing tough ask to end 57 years of Open hurt
News.content:
Never mind Bryson DeChambeau stomping around in the rough as he improved his lie, for so long this Open Saturday turned into Tommy Fleetwood walking in his Royal Birkdale wonderland as he enhanced the mood of seemingly everyone in attendance.

Alas, the fun could not last and, even though he still has a chance of becoming England’s first Open winner on English soil since 1969, that finish looked costly. Fifty-seven years of hurt and all that...

On five under, Fleetwood is in a tie for ninth, five off the lead held by Sam Burns, the American who, after a 65, is two clear of New Zealander Ryan Fox and South Korean Kim Si-woo. DeChambeau is alongside Swede Ludvig Aberg, in a tie for sixth on six under, after a 69.

He was heckled on the 18th because of the two-shot penalty he received on Friday night for “inadvertently improving his lie” on the fifth. “You’re a cheat, Bryson,” the fan shouted.

It was a sour point that was in no way in keeping with the mood of this Saturday that had been overwhelmingly positive. With Fleetwood as the focus, of course.

The enormous crowd cheered and sang and backed their fellow Merseysider all the way as Fleetwood launched his charge into contention at this Southport links which he would once sneak on as a child. His playing partner, Jon Rahm, was taken aback by the level of support.

“The best way I can explain it, it was so intense that, without meaning any disrespect I’m glad England didn’t win the semi-final [of the World Cup] because I would have been having a heck of a three days with the fans if they had been playing Spain in tomorrow’s final,” Rahm said.

Sports.title: World Cup final LIVE: Post-match brawl breaks out as Spain crowned champions vs Argentina
Sports.content:
Spain have been crowned the champions of the world two years after securing the European crown having dominated Argentina in the final in New Jersey, with Ferran Torres' goal enough

Spain have won the World Cup with a slender victory against Argentina in New Jersey.

Ferran Torres gave the European champions the lead just minutes into the second period of extra time. His goal came after nearly two hours of goalless football at MetLife Stadium. Argentina were reduced to ten men before the extra 30 minutes, with Chelsea's Enzo Fernandez sent off for two bookable offence.

There was also some drama before the game. Spain's pre-match training session was forced to be cancelled due to storms, while fans and members of the media have stumbled into serious issues getting into the stadium. Meanwhile, the pre-match closing ceremonies have ran over, with delays impacting the game itself.

Sports.title: Spain vs Argentina player ratings as Enzo Fernandez costs his side the World Cup final
Sports.content:
Spain have won the World Cup for the second time after beating a dour Argentina side 1-0 after extra time in the final.

After the pageantry before kick-off, the first half was an extremely cagey affair with Lamine Yamal going closest. Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez then suffered heartache shortly before the break when he was forced off with an injury.

Both sides then had to sit in their respective dressing room for a relative eternity as the World Cup final was paused for the much-feted half-time show.

It was much of the same once they did appear though, with Spain dominating possession but failing to carve out any gilt-edge chances.

‌



As extra time loomed, Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez was shown red after flying into a tackle already on a yellow card.

Sports.title: World Cup final ends in chaos as Argentina star throws punches after Spain win
Sports.content:
World Cup final ends in chaos as Argentina star throws punches after Spain win

Punches were thrown at full time of the World Cup final after Spain defeated Argentina thanks to Ferran Torres' goal in extra time at MetLife Stadium

View 3 Images Players clashed after Spain beat Argentina in the 2026 FIFA World Cup final

Spain's World Cup win over Argentina was marred by unsavoury scenes at the full-time whistle, with punches thrown. Leandro Paredes was sent off following the whistle, while Molina also appeared to throw a punch after the match.

The latter took a swing at Rodri, while Paredes was spotted kicking Eric Garcia to the floor before pushing him back with a hand around his neck when the Barcelona defender attempted to confront him. He was also spotted in an exchange with Gavi.

Chaos reigned as Spain went into jubilant celebrations elsewhere on the pitch.

‌



"Paredes threw two or three haymakers into someone's face. He went for them," said Alan Shearer. "There is no place or space for that.

"We know how much it means to them and we know how much it hurts to lose, but there is a way to lose. Too many times we have seen that from Argentina. The reaction after the final whistle is terrible."

Lionel Messi slammed for desperate attempt to get Spain star sent off in World Cup final READ MORE :

World Cup fans issue the same complaint about half-time show as Spain vs Argentina delayed READ MORE :

Gary Neville had a simple assessment. "I love the competitiveness of the Argentines but Paredes has been a disgrace the last couple of games," he said.

Wayne Rooney was not surprised by how Argentina handled the defeat. He said: "Does is surprise you? It doesn't surprise me, I think we've seen this with Argentina before and it's just not the reaction you want.

"We've seen some of the reaction after knocking England out in the last round as well. I think Enzo Fernandez has got what he deserves as well, so it's disappointing. But that's just sad. If you lose a game of football, be graceful and get out of there. It's very poor from them."

View 3 Images The World Cup final ended in chaos (Image: TV)

‌



Ex-England goalkeeper Joe Hart added: "Disgusting. There was one man on the pitch who did have class, and that was Lionel Mess - shook hands of every one of those Spanish players.

"The game's done, they can have absolutely no complaints about what happened today. Disgusting behaviour.

"Rodri, I don't think, needed to get in their faces, but when you've been wound up for 120 minutes, and you felt you've been wronged, and you've felt the referee's on your back, and you've got that win, referee's blown his whistle, leave it. And I think Argentina...are you surprised they've gone over the line again?"

‌



Micah Richards ensured that the pundits were unanimous in their assessment. He said: "The first yellow card wasn't until 40 odd minutes in the first-half, but seeing that sort of stuff after the game's been played and someone's just been crowned World Cup champions, it's not good enough.

View 3 Images Leandro Paredes and Eric Garcia have words after the FIFA World Cup 2026 Final match (Image: Al Bello/Getty Images)

"It's quite embarrassing to be honest. Paraedes there, he doesn't need to do that, he's better than that.

‌



"And it doesn't stop there, it keeps going, and going, and going. And we all know what it's like to lose a game, we can be very frustrated, we understand that. But this is not good enough, it's not a good look at all."

The fiery end followed a game where Paredes was lucky to stay on the pitch, despite only entering the field at half-time. The Argentina star was lucky to stay on the field after a number of questionable challenges.

The World Cup runners-up saw Enzo Fernandez sent off in the 93rd minute of the match, leaving them with a one-man disadvantage heading into extra time. A tense tie was eventually separated by Ferran Torres as the European team became world champions for the first time since 2010.

Sports.title: Spain beat Argentina in World Cup final after Enzo Fernandez's moment of madness - 5 talking points
Sports.content:
Ferran Torres was in the right place at the right time to mercifully settle a drab World Cup final in extra-time as Spain's dominance finally told against Argentina in New Jersey.

The reigning world champions, chasing history as they sought to become just the third team to ever win successive World Cups, failed to show up. Even with the genius of Lionel Messi in tow, Argentina were toothless on the biggest stage, failing to muster a single shot on goal until the 117th minute.

An uneventful first half slowly turned into a lulling Spain siege with Emi Martinez called into action to thwart Dani Olmo. It was the Aston Villa star keeping Argentina alive, making saves from Torres, Aymeric Laporte and numerous others as Spain increased the pressure.

Then, with extra-time looming, Enzo Fernandez was shown a second yellow card after the Chelsea midfielder went flying into Pau Cubarsi in a 50-50 near halfway to leave Argentina with a mountain to climb.

‌



Spain thought they finally had the goal their play merited in the early minutes of extra-time when Nico Williams smuggled the ball into the back of the net through a sea of bodies in the box before it was chalked off. But Argentina and Martinez's resistance was finally broken in the 106th minute when Torres plundered the winning goal.

Here are Mirror Football's talking points from the World Cup final...

World Cup final LIVE: Spain vs Argentina match and goal updates as Martinez suffers injury blow READ MORE :

Lisandro Martinez in floods of tears as Man Utd star suffers World Cup final agony READ MORE :

1. Argentina's fortune continues...until it doesn't

Unless you've been living under a rock for the last month, you'll probably be aware that Argentina have benefitted from some favourable officiating decisions. Egypt, eliminated in the most heartbreaking yet epic fashion by the defending world champions in the round of 16, even alleged there was a bias towards Lionel Scaloni's side from Fifa.

There were more than a few circumstances during the England-Argentina game where those in blue and white stripes were fortunate to avoid being reprimanded by the officials. And wherever you stand on such talk, Alexis Mac Allister escaping punishment for a late, reckless challenge on Dani Olmo early in the first half will do little to stifle such accusations.

‌



Maybe Argentina have just had the rub of the green on their way to tonight's final. But more than a few incidents during their enthralling run to the final, including Mac Allister's escape and the decision to rule out a Williams goal in extra-time for a soft foul on Nico Otamendi, have left an extremely sour taste.

2. A slow burn

View 5 Images Alexis Mac Allister was fortunate to escape punishment for a reckless challenge on Dani Olmo (Image: Daniela Porcelli)

Pre-match, the big question on the BBC's coverage of the final was over who would be the unfortunate soul to follow Jennifer Hudson and her epic performance of the American national anthem. But perhaps the real concern should have been over this match following the 10-goal thriller England and France served up in their bronze final less than 24 hours earlier.

Alright, the occasion isn't comparable and nerves and tension will have undoubtedly played a part in a drab first half, which saw the fewest shots (three, all for Spain) in any half of a World Cup final in history.

‌



For all the razzmatazz of the United States' big plans for its pre-match coverage, not to mention a half-time show, the action on the pitch didn't live up to the billing here. Even with an additional half an hour of play.

3. Fernandez's moment of madness

View 5 Images Enzo Fernandez was sent off in the final minutes of normal time

Not even Argentina and their good fortune could survive Fernandez and his stupid decision to go absolutely hurtling into Cubarsi in the final moments of extra-time. Already on a yellow card for dissent, there could only be one outcome.

Considering Argentina were pretty much under the pump for the whole game, Fernandez's cheap dismissal felt like the death knell for their chances of becoming just the third nation in history to win successive World Cups.

‌



Fernandez was distraught, but it was an absolute moment of madness from a player who rescued Argentina in their hour of need just days beforehand. If Fernandez saved Argentina's World Cup hopes with his stunner against England, then he absolutely killed them here.

4. Martinez's one-man stand v Spain

View 5 Images Emi Martinez kept Argentina alive in the World Cup final with save after save (Image: Marvin Ibo Guengoer/GES Sportfoto)

Spain dominated the game in regulation time when both sides had 11 men, so there was an air of inevitably about Spain's winning goal when it eventually did come in extra-time. But if one man on the pitch didn't deserve to be on the losing side, it was Martinez.

Heroic in Qatar four years ago as Argentina bested France on penalties, Martinez produced a performance on par with that in New Jersey, even if it was not enough to lift his country to yet more history.

‌



After springing to the turf to repel another Spain attempt, Martinez turned to whip up the crowd shortly after Fernandez's dismissal. But even Argentina's larger than life keeper was unable to deny Torres' powerful effort, Martinez finally beaten at the 12th attempt.

5. The Messi-Yamal final falls flat

View 5 Images Lionel Messi and Lamine Yamal faced off in New Jersey (Image: Alex Livesey/Danehouse)

We've all seen the picture; that one of Messi crading a baby Yamal taken when the Argentine magician was a teenager with the world at his feet. This was the dream final that Fifa would have privately craved months ago: the one that pitted master vs apprentice, Messi against Yamal. Narrative wise, it was pitch-perfect.

Unfortunately, it transpired to be anything but. Both were ineffective and bystanders for large periods as Spain and Argentina sparred nervously for more than two hours.

‌



This has been a tournament where Messi, even at 39 years of age, has cemented has reputation as the world's undisputed best, orchestrating resurrections against Cape Verde, Egypt and England to propel Argentina to a second successive World Cup final. But their tournament ended with a whimper here; Argentina were practically non-existent as an attacking force, failing to muster a single attempt on goal in regulation time. This was a meek surrender.

In the case of Yamal, there were flashes of the genius that will almost certainly ensure he enjoys a long, fruitful reign as one of football's new icons. But like Messi, he too was on the periphery for much of this final. In truth, it's been that sort of tournament for Messi's Barcelona heir.

This World Cup will be remembered for many things. Unfortunately, the Messi-Yamal final will not be one of them.

World Cup Golden Boot winner confirmed after Kylian Mbappe and Lionel Messi battle

Kylian Mbappe has won the race for the 2026 World Cup Golden Boot, finishing the competition on 10 goals after a stellar tournament in North America. That's despite Lionel Messi having a major advantage in the opportunity to bolster his own tally of eight during Sunday's final against Spain.

‌



The 39-year-old was unable to do so, however, with his nation suffering heartbreak at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey in the form of a 1-0 loss in extra-time. Ferran Torres broke the deadlock for the European champions 106 minutes into play, not only to give his nation the lead, but ultimately win the match.

‌



It was a remarkable tournament for Mbappe, who proved himself once more on the world stage in North America. The 27-year-old kickstarted his tournament with a boom last month, bagging a brace in a 3-1 opening day win with France against Senegal.

Sports.title: Spain overwhelm dismal Argentina to win the World Cup for second time
Sports.content:
Finally justice was done in the MetLife Stadium.

The one team who came to play football won against the kings of anti-football.

Ferran Torres was Spain’s hero even if it needed extra time to see off Lionel Messi and Co as holders Argentina lost their grip on the World Cup trophy.

Messi’s dreams were left in tatters as this did not feel a remotely fitting way for one of football’s greatest players of all time to bow out if this proves to be his final act for his country.

‌



Argentina were dreadful, they did not manage a single shot on target and it felt as if they had no ambition to win the game. Enzo Fernandez was sent off in injury time at the end of 90 minutes and that just about summed up their ugly, spoiling and nasty approach.

And Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes greeted the final whistle by sparking a melee and swinging punches at celebrating Spain stars.

Wayne Rooney leaves BBC pundits speechless with brutal review of World Cup half-time show READ MORE :

Donald Trump brutally booed at World Cup final as Spain and Argentina fans unite READ MORE :

In contrast, Spain ushered in a new world order as the European champions now rule the world and they were utterly dominant in a final which did not really live up to its billing.

They thoroughly deserved their win and their stylish football helped us focus on the pitch and forget the silly showbiz that FIFA tried to impose on their showcase game.

‌



Spain had so many chances, so many near misses and Emiliano Martinez was Argentina’s hero with an incredible performance as he produced at least a dozen saves.

That is the one flaw in Spain’s make-up - they do not have a goal poacher who can finish off their wonderful, free-flowing approach play.

It needed a flick on from Nico Williams to set up Torres to finally seal the victory which sparked wild scenes of celebrations among the sea of red shirts in the crowd.

This was their day and a victory for football over spoilers but also helped the purists savour the game and quickly forget about lavish pre-match and half time shows.

‌



View 4 Images Lionel Messi during the World Cup final between Spain and Argentina

They had music, light shows and a bizarre half set which left most of the crowd cold amid the blazing sun in New Jersey.

The true football fans had come for the game and Argentina had just run out of dirty tricks, energy and legs after their exertions against England.

Mind you, Thomas Tuchel’s men must have been watching on from holiday and be thinking they would have given a better account of themselves than Argentina.

‌



They were woeful. Never looked like retaining their trophy - they wanted to become the first team since Brazil in 1962 to do that - and they looked a spent force.

View 4 Images Spain are champions of the world for the second time

Spain were bright, dominant and Rodri conducted them from midfield as they created chance after chance but were thwarted by Martinez.

Lamine Yamal did not really step up but had a good game and yet they just could not score. Lisandro Martinez went off injured for Argentina and they became the walking wounded after so many comebacks in this World Cup.

‌



Pedri, Torres and Mikel Merino all went close while Williams had an effort ruled out as you began to wonder whether they would score.

Even after Fernandez’s red card - for a second yellow after a foul on Pau Cubarsí - did not help Spain as Argentina dug in to try and hold on for penalties.

View 4 Images Enzo Fernandez was shown a red card in the closing stages of normal time

It felt like it was heading that way until Torres’ intervention. Then - and only then - did we see signs of life from Argentina.

‌



They pushed, Messi tried and they went close but Spain were superior and deserved their win.

This Argentina side looked to have reached the end of the road. Too many ageing players. Surely Messi will call it quits at 39 or he will certainly retire before the next World Cup.

Mentality and fight has carried them a long way in this tournament - and that is to be admired. If only England had as much.

But they were undone by a much better footballing side and Spain are now kings of the world again. And deservedly so.

‌

Sports.title: Lionel Messi slammed for desperate attempt to get Spain star sent off in World Cup final
Sports.content:
Lionel Messi slammed for desperate attempt to get Spain star sent off in World Cup final

Enzo Fernandez was sent off for Argentina during stoppage time in their World Cup final clash with Spain, but Lionel Messi also tried to get a Spain star red carded during the clash

View Image Lionel Messi tried to get Marc Cucurella sent off during the World Cup final (Image: BBC)

Lionel Messi was slammed by Wayne Rooney, Micah Richards and Joe Hart for trying to get Marc Cucurella sent off in sly fashion during the World Cup final. A moment of excitement sparked late into Argentina's clash with Spain at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, following a largely lacklustre 90 minutes, when Enzo Fernandez was given an early exit.

‌



The Chelsea star, who was already on a yellow for dissent earlier in the match, bundled through Pau Curbasi needlessly during stoppage time, sending him feet into the air with a dangling leg and leaving him in a heap on the floor. Referee Slavko Vincic didn't hesitate as he showed Fernandez a red card for the cynical foul, with immediate protests from the 25-year-old.

‌



However, it was during the furore that Messi attempted to immediately level the playing field by getting Cucurella sent off. Replays showed the Real Madrid full-back somewhat raising his hand to his face as he conversed with the Argentine captain.

‌



Donald Trump picks his World Cup winner and makes request to Gianni Infantino READ MORE :

Alan Shearer lets rip at 'stupid' Enzo Fernandez sent off in Spain vs Argentina World Cup final READ MORE :

While his mouth wasn't fully covered, a new rule from FIFA in a bid to rub out racism has been implemented for this summer's tournament, which prevents players from speaking to opponents with their mouths covered.

And while Cucurella may not have said anything sinister as he conversed with the 39-year-old, Messi was quick to flag to officials that Cucurella had covered his mouth.

The forward's pleas ultimately fell on deaf ears, however, as no action was taken against Cucurella.

‌



And as the two sides headed into extra time, the BBC panel of Rooney, Richards, Hart and Gabby Logan voiced their frustrations with the showing from one of the world's most respected players.

‌



Shocked by the move, Richards replied: "He's not got his whole hand over, he's got two fingers. It's harsh isn't it? You don't want to see people getting sent off in a World Cup final for that."

Hart then gave his two cents as he added: "Yeah, I didn't enjoy that at all.

"You realise how on top Spain are in this game if even Lionel Messi is reverting to that," before Logan replied: "Desperation from Messi there?"

Sports.title: Spain claim World Cup victory over Argentina after Torres' extra-time winner
Sports.content:
Spain won their second World Cup title after Ferran Torres' 106th-minute smashed finish earned a 1-0 win against defending champions Argentina in the 2026 final.

The win had shades of their maiden victory in 2010 too - scoring in the second period of extra time after a goalless 90 minutes. Then, it was Andres Iniesta against the Netherlands - now another Barcelona player, Torres, adds his name to the history books.

It was a nod back from fellow substitute Nico Williams that saw the former Manchester City forward storm on to the ball and fire past Aston Villa goalkeeper Emi Martinez. It came minutes after Williams had an initial strike ruled out for a Mikel Merino foul on Nicolas Otamendi.

It was no less than Spain deserved either, having been the far better team on the night. The game is perhaps summed up in the shot count - La Roja had 20 while Argentina registered two, and even those were late in extra time. One of those was a skied effort from Giuliano Simeone that could have sent the game to penalties.

Argentina did keep their shape well as Spain applied consistent pressure - especially after Chelsea's Enzo Fernandez was sent off for a reckless second yellow at the end of normal time - and relied on Martinez to make a string of saves.

Image: Enzo Fernandez fouls Pau Cubarsi resulting in a red card for the Argentina midfielder

Image: Enzo Fernandez was sent off late in the second half as Argentina finished the game with ten players

But there is no fairytale end to Lionel Messi's expected final World Cup appearance, with the Argentina skipper anonymous for much of the game with his team unable to get hold of the ball. He is also beaten to his first World Cup Golden Boot by France's Kylian Mbappe, who won it by two goals.

For Spain, they remain undefeated under manager Luis de la Fuente in competitive matches, adding a World Cup win to their Euros title from 2024. It has been quite the tournament from an opening draw to Cape Verde to making France and Argentina look like average teams.

And as numerous players from the victorious squad of 16 years ago watched on, it was another nod to their achievements when they also followed up their Euro 2008 victory with the World Cup trophy in South Africa.

Paredes and Molina involved full-time after angry scenes

There were unsavoury scenes at full-time as Leandro Paredes and Nahuel Molina looked to strike out at the celebrating Spain players after Argentina's defeat.

Molina threw out an elbow and caught Rodri, while Paredes appeared to kick Eric Garcia to the floor and pushed him back with a strong hand around his neck when the Spaniard got back to his feet to confront him.

A Spain substitute was then held back by another Argentina player, before Paredes came in, ripped his bib and swung for him twice, catching him in the face.

Paredes, who came on at half-time, was booked within minutes of coming on and escaped a number of other yellow card offenses.

Image: Spain's Ferran Torres celebrates scoring their winner (AP Photo/Julio Cortez)

5: SHOT! Lamine Yamal has the first shot on target.

39: SHOT! Oyarzabal strikes - but it goes straight at Emi Martinez.

77: CHANCE! Pedro and Pau Cubarsi draw saves from the Argentina goalkeeper as Spain keep pushing for a goal.

90+3: RED CARD! Fernandez sent off for second yellow card after reckless challenge on Cubarsi.

90+9: SAVE! Lamine Yamal forces a great save from Emi Martinez after a whipped effort.

96: NO GOAL! Williams has the ball in the net, but it is ruled out as Merino inadvertently catches Otamendi on the foot in the build-up.

106: GOAL! Torres fires home from Williams' cushioned effort.

114: OFFSIDE! Torres has the ball in the net again, but he is flagged offside.

120+2: OVER! Simeone has the chance to equalise, but sends an effort over the face of goal as Spain win the World Cup.

Image: Spain's Nico Williams reacts after seeing his strike on goal ruled out by VAR

Analysis: Spain worthy World Cup winners

Sky Sports' Adam Bate: "Spain began this World Cup with a goalless draw against Cape Verde but they end it as worthy winners. They beat the favourites in the semi-final and the reigning champions tonight.

"One goal conceded in eight games, never behind in the tournament, they played all the football here. Passed Argentina off the park. The European champions are World Cup winners too. Thoroughly deserved."

Sky Sports' Gary Neville speaking on ITV: "Spain are not the best individual players, what they are is the best team, the best collective. And also the best system of play.

"I spent a very short time in Spain and what I found was that they were a different technical and tactical level to Premier League teams, their understanding of the game.

"That comes out most in international football when you are playing every four days in 35 degree heat. Technically and tactically, they are outstanding."

Sports.title: 'My hands were all over the place!' - Fox savours dramatic Open win
Sports.content:
Ryan Fox admitted it was a "dream come true" as he defied the nerves to clinch a dramatic victory in The Open at Royal Birkdale.

The 39-year-old New Zealander produced a superb finish to the final round to overtake clubhouse leader Cameron Young and snatch a one-shot win.

Fox, who had carded a 62 on Saturday to put himself in contention to claim a maiden major success, looked to be slipping out of it after making his second bogey of the day at the 11th.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the final round of the 154th Open as Fox claimed the victory

Back-to-back birdies at the 13th and 14th put him back in the hunt and he then did well to escape with only a bogey at the 15th after a nightmare lie in a greenside bunker.

He hit back by birdieing the 16th following a brilliant approach and then, after missing a chance at the 17th, nailed two superb shots down the 18th before boldly draining a 12-foot putt to claim the Claret Jug.

"To play that last hole how I did, I stood on the tee and said to my caddie Dean (Smith), we're going to try to win this," said Fox.

"I hit two perfect shots. I'm not sure how I hit the putt. My hands were all over the place. I was just trying to get it towards the hole somewhere. It's surreal that it went in.

"My focus with the putter all day was just take a really deep breath before I hit it and just try to hit a line, and I did that.

Image: Fox celebrates after holing the winning putt

"I don't know how I managed to keep the putter face square enough for that to go on line, but I'll take it.

"Champion Golfer of the Year has got a pretty good ring to it. It is a dream come true.

"You do dream of this moment. I don't know whether I ever thought it was going to become a reality. Now it is, and to have my name etched in the history of the game is pretty awesome. I think it's pretty awesome for New Zealand as well. It's going to be big down there."

Fox is the son of former All Blacks fly-half Grant Fox and the grandson of former New Zealand Test captain Merv Wallace.

"We've got a great history in our family," he said. "I was lucky enough to carve my own path there. I don't know if this tops their achievements, but it's certainly right up there.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Fox equalled the lowest round in Open history with a third-round 62 at Royal Birkdale

"I spoke to my kids last night, and they said bring back a trophy. I think this is a pretty cool one to bring back for them.

"I don't know if my dad would be able to contain himself when I was coming down the stretch. He's never been one who has been very good if he doesn't have control over things.

"I think when he was playing and in control of the output, under pressure he was fine. But when he doesn't have control, I think he's a nervous wreck. I'm sure he was."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player How Fox clinched victory in The Open at Royal Birkdale

'He stayed aggressive'

Sky Sports Golf duo Dame Laura Davies and Andrew Coltart were both full of praise for Fox and the aggressive approach he adopted on the back nine.

Davies said: "He was the most impressive player all day. He stayed aggressive; I don't think he was scared of losing it. If he lost it because he hit a shot that just didn't work out he was prepared to stay aggressive and I firmly believe that's why he did it.

"He hit irons when he had to, but when there was a chance, a sniff of a birdie, the driver was out, full commitment.

"And the way he played 18 I don't think you could have drawn that up any better. Two of the best shots he will ever hit in his life just to hit that green to give himself a chance."

Image: Fox proudly holds the Claret Jug

Coltart added: "I've never seen somebody push through the tape as hard as that right at the end of the tournament to win a major championship.

"At a place like this, too. It was just superb. The 62 on Saturday I think, helped cement his belief in his ability out there.

"While they all struggled with the pressure, he stood tall."

Sports.title: 'My heart really sank' - Hamilton relieved mechanic unhurt after hit
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton says his "heart really sank" when his Ferrari hit a mechanic in a pit-stop incident that led to the team being fined heavily by Belgian Grand Prix stewards.

Hamilton's right-front tyre struck the mechanic - who was unhurt - after the driver was given the green signal to leave the team's pit box, briefly knocking the crew member, who was in front of the wheel in an attempt to make a front-wing adjustment, to his knees.

Hamilton promptly stopped his car as the mechanic was helped to his feet, before leaving the pit box.

The incident was placed under a post-race stewards' investigation with Ferrari later handed a €30,000 fine, €10,000 of which is suspended for a year.

Ferrari admitted to an "inappropriately late instruction for the wing adjustment, a lack of clear communication and the mechanic's failure to notice the green light" amid a "complex and unusual combination of circumstances" at a stop which Hamilton had first served a five-second penalty before work on the car commenced.

With no fault attributed to the driver, who stewards said had also suffered a "sporting disadvantage" anyway due to the fact he was delayed in leaving the pit stop, Hamilton retained his fourth-place finish in the race.

The result moved Hamilton back into second place ahead of George Russell in the Drivers' Championship with a deficit of 45 points to Kimi Antonelli, the race winner at Spa-Francorchamps.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Belgian Grand Prix

Speaking about the pit stop confusion after the race, Hamilton said his mind had immediately flashed back to an incident at the 2018 Bahrain Grand Prix when a botched Ferrari stop for Kimi Raikkonen caused a mechanic, Francesco Cigarini, to suffer a double leg fracture.

Hamilton was therefore relieved to be told that the mechanic involved on Sunday was not injured, when he enquired about him over team radio.

"The green light went and so I went," said Hamilton to Sky Sports F1.

"You're looking over here [to the left at the lights] you're not looking over there so that's more probably on the team, ultimately.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Despite being given a five-second penalty for an opening lap collision with George Russell, Lewis Hamilton was left more frustrated with his performance over the weekend as he finished fourth in Belgium

"But when it happened, then I noticed him and I stopped and it just went through my mind in that moment was back when Kimi hit and [a mechanic] broke a leg and my heart really sank for a second.

"I'm really grateful he's OK."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton crashes at Turn 13 during the final practice session at the Belgian GP

'We could have been challenging for the win' - Hamilton rues consequence of his Saturday crash

Hamilton's stop had already been elongated by the fact that Ferrari's crew had first had to wait five seconds before starting the car's tyre change owing to the serving of a time penalty for causing a collision with Russell at Les Combes on the opening lap.

The clash spun Russell out of the race, although the Mercedes driver later blamed his own car's straight-line speed issues, rather than former team-mate Hamilton, for the incident at the end of the long Kemmel Straight.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch from onboard with George Russell as he crashes out of the Belgian GP after contact with Lewis Hamilton

Hamilton also preferred not to focus on the specifics of the collision in his post-race interview, instead taking the blame for not qualifying higher than sixth, which became fifth on the grid due to Lando Norris' engine penalty, after crashing in Saturday's final practice session.

"I don't count on myself [being] unlucky, I think about my mistake that I made yesterday, so I take full responsibility really for the fourth place that I ended up getting," he said.

"I damaged the car then when they rebuilt the car they missed something on the suspension so the balance was completely different so it meant I was probably a good couple of tenths - maybe three tenths - slower than I should have been in qualifying.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Drama at the start of the Belgium GP as George Russell's title hopes take a huge blow

"Then I ended up further back, got in the incident. Five second penalty, so like a domino effect from a mistake from myself.

"But the team have been doing a great job with strategy, pit stops. We are continuing to improve the car. I think our pace today, without the damage, we could have been challenging for the win."
