Sports.title: Antonelli takes big Belgian GP win as Russell's title woes deepen
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli overcame an unfortunately-timed Virtual Safety Car to overtake Charles Leclerc and win the Belgian Grand Prix on a day team-mate George Russell's title hopes suffered a major fresh setback.

Antonelli doubled his in-house advantage over Russell to 50 points after the Briton was spun out into the gravel at the fifth corner of the first lap in a collision with Lewis Hamilton that stewards judged the Ferrari driver at fault for.

Hamilton was given a five-second penalty, which he served at his sole pit stop, and eventually finished fourth after overtaking McLaren's Oscar Piastri with four laps to go.

Hamilton and Ferrari faced a post-race investigation for an unsafe Ferrari release at the same pit stop.

A mechanic was struck by the Ferrari's front-right tyre and was briefly knocked to his knees after Hamilton was incorrectly given the signal to leave his pit box. The mechanic was unhurt.

Ferrari were fined €30,000, of which a third of the amount was suspended for 12 months, for the incident.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The Ferrari pit crew were unable to adjust Lewis Hamilton's front wing as the British driver knocked over a mechanic after being given the green light

Hamilton moves back ahead of Russell to second behind Antonelli in the standings - 45 points behind the Italian, whose sixth victory of the season reinforces his championship favourite status with one race to go in Hungary this coming week before Formula 1's summer break after Mercedes unreliability had struck his car in two of the previous three races.

Max Verstappen, who briefly took the lead from Antonelli on the first lap into Eau Rouge before the Mercedes almost immediately blasted back past, took third after he was also jumped by Leclerc during the VSC.

The Dutchman struggled on the hard tyres in the final stint and finished nine seconds behind Leclerc for Red Bull's 300th podium finish in F1.

Isack Hadjar drove strongly to finish sixth in the second Red Bull from the back row, opportunistically making two pit stops under the early Safety Car for Russell's crash to fulfil the mandatory race-tyre requirements.

Hadjar just held off Lando Norris, who was on significantly fresher tyres, after the McLaren had run to lap 30 before making his one pit stop having started a penalised 13th on the grid.

Gabriel Bortoleto was eighth for Audi ahead of Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad and Alpine's Franco Colapinto.

Belgian GP Result: Top 10 1) Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes



2) Charles Leclerc, Ferrari



3) Max Verstappen, Red Bull



4) Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari



5) Oscar Piastri, McLaren



6) Isack Hadjar, Red Bull



7) Lando Norris, McLaren



8) Gabriel Bortoleto, Audi



9) Arvid Lindblad, Racing Bulls



10) Franco Colapinto, Alpine

How faultless Antonelli was made to win the hard way

Mercedes' world championship leader had been the big favourite to win the race after qualifying on a dominant pole position but the 19-year-old's route to victory on Sunday did not prove quite as straightforward as many had expected across a tense 44 laps of racing at Spa-Francorchamps.

Antonelli had, though, always been braced for a battle to hold on to his lead through the first lap of the race from fellow front-row-starter Verstappen due to the slipstream-friendly nature of the opening part of the undulating, power-sensitive Belgian lap.

He stayed ahead on the short initial run to La Source but, amid different stages of energy deployment, was overtaken by Verstappen as they arrived at the bottom of Eau Rouge.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Drama at the start of the Belgium GP as George Russell's title hopes take a huge blow

But Antonelli had more battery power in hand for the long Kemmel Straight and duly breezed straight back past the Red Bull before the next braking zone of Les Combes.

Leclerc, meanwhile, had made an impressive start from fourth place and passed Verstappen too.

Verstappen got back ahead of the Ferrari for second place on lap six and, impressively so given the pre-race expectations had been that Antonelli would run and hide, managed to keep the leading Mercedes in view. He was less than three seconds behind Antonelli when he pitted first on lap 17.

Antonelli stopped a lap later and stayed ahead of the Red Bull to maintain the net race lead.

But Ferrari had kept both their drivers out for longer and benefitted when, on lap 20, the Virtual Safety Car was initiated for debris on track.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mercedes Kimi Antonelli discusses his Belgian GP win and admits he's in a 'good position' after opening up a 45-point gap in the drivers' standings.

With the cars on circuit forced to run at reduced speed, Ferrari were able to pit their drivers simultaneously while losing less race time compared to a non-VSC stop.

It worked a treat as Leclerc had jumped both Verstappen and Antonelli on his return to the circuit.

However, Hamilton, who first had to serve his five-second penalty before his tyre change could commence, was further delayed when confusion led to the mechanic who had been asked to adjust his front wing being knocked over when the Briton incorrectly got the green light to leave the box.

Leclerc re-emerged 2.5 seconds ahead of Antonelli and with the apparent advantage of slightly fresher hard tyres.

But the Mercedes simply had too much speed and, unlike two weeks before at Silverstone when the Silver Arrow ran into technical trouble just as it appeared poised to overtake the Ferrari for the lead, Antonelli on lap 34 moved ahead of Leclerc down the Kemmel Straight.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Oscar Piastri takes to his McLaren team radio to complain about contact with Ferrari's Charles Leclerc.

Not that Mercedes simply breezed away from Ferrari thereafter, Antonelli eventually taking the chequered flag just 1.9s ahead of Leclerc to secure a narrow but significant win given the context of both his recent misfortune and Russell's early exit here.

"It's great to be back on the top step after obviously a few difficult rounds," said Antonelli. "It was a hard-fought race. We lost first place with a VSC but then we managed to make our way back.

"It was a tough win because Charles was quick and we had to hold onto them."

Second place followed Leclerc's victory at Silverstone amid a resurgence in his form, and the Monegasque said: "I believed in the win until the end. We had a little bit of luck with the VSC at the right time for us but the pace was relatively strong.

"There were five or six laps on the hard tyres when I was struggling with the front axle, then it came back a little bit."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell pointed to an issue with the car as a reason for his collision with Lewis Hamilton during the Belgian GP

Russell bemoans Mercedes straight-line speed issues after Hamilton tangle

Race day could barely have gone any worse for a frustrated Russell in the other title-contending Mercedes car.

The Briton had qualified third, a position he held until the Kemmel Straight on lap one when both Ferraris drafted past him and he came under attack from Piastri's McLaren too.

Russell attempted to come back at Hamilton on the outside of his compatriot under braking for the right-handed turn into Les Combes, but the Ferrari understeered and tagged the Mercedes' right-rear wheel, spinning it round into the gravel.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch from onboard with George Russell as he crashes out of the Belgian GP after contact with Lewis Hamilton.

Stewards may have penalised Hamilton for the incident, but Russell instead took issue with the mysterious straight-line speed issues that had dogged his Mercedes all weekend.

"I just got totally swallowed up down the straight," said a dejected Russell.

"I lost three positions down the straight down into Turn Five and then the incident was a racing incident.

"Maybe I could have gone a bit wider, maybe he (Hamilton) could have braked a bit more. The incident shouldn't have happened if I had the speed down the straight."

Sports.title: England clinch India series in Lord's run-fest
Sports.content:
Ben Duckett's century and Sam Curran's late burst of wickets inspired England to a series-clinching 27-run win over India in the third ODI at Lord's.

Duckett struck a magnificent 141 from 135 balls, the highest individual ODI score at Lord's and his fourth century in the format, before a swashbuckling 41 from just 13 balls by Jos Buttler helped England set India a daunting 388 to win.

Rohit Sharma led the chase with a superb 138 off 110 deliveries, registering his 34th ODI hundred and sharing century partnerships with Shubman Gill (77) and Virat Kohli (74) to keep India firmly on course.

England vs India, third ODI, Lord’s England 387-3 after 50 overs (chose to bat): Ben Duckett (141 off 135), Jacob Bethell (91 off 93), Joe Root (74 off 48), Jos Buttler (41 off 13); Prasidh Krishna (2-69), Prince Yadav (1-79) India 260-7 after 50 overs: Rohit Sharma (138 off 110), Shubman Gill (77 off 84), Virat Kohli (74 off 60); Sam Curran (4-75), Jacob Bethell (1-49), Jofra Archer (1-63) Adil Rashid (1-64)

India were 303-2 and needed 84 from the final 39 balls when a decisive seven-ball spell saw Curran (4-75) dismiss Ishan Kishan (14), Shreyas Iyer (0) and Kohli, halting India's momentum as their chase fell 27 runs short.

After losing the series opener by six wickets at Edgbaston, England bounced back to secure a 2-1 ODI series victory over the world's top-ranked side, adding it to their 4-0 T20 series whitewash of India.

How England clinched ODI series victory over India

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ben Duckett puts on a dominant display against India as he bats an amazing 141

Harry Brook completed a clean sweep of successful tosses with his third of the series, and his decision to bat paid immediate dividends as England's openers feasted on an Indian attack left rudderless without injured pace talisman Jasprit Bumrah.

India were made to toil in the field as England recorded a record 192-run first-wicket stand before Bethell picked out Rohit Sharma at cow corner to fall nine runs short of an emotional century on the day Lord's remembered Sir Garfield Sobers.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jacob Bethell is dismissed for 90 as he bats a superb innings in England's third ODI match against India

Duckett kicked on after reaching his century, blasting 18 fours and a six to surpass Sir Viv Richards' 138 not out against England in 1979 and register a new highest individual score in a Lord's ODI before falling caught and bowled to Prince Yadav.

Joe Root hit a sixth successive ODI half-century after Duckett's dismissal before Jos Buttler's four fours and three sixes in a blistering late cameo saw England plunder 82 runs from the final five overs to finish on 387-3 after 50 overs of domination with the bat.

It left India needing to pull off the second-highest run chase in ODI history to win the series, but confidence grew that it could be possible when Rohit and Gill put on a 147-run opening stand.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ben Duckett puts on a dominant display against India as he bats an amazing 141

Gill suffered a recurrence of the cramp that forced him to retire in the first ODI at Edgbaston, and four overs after receiving treatment the India captain was trapped lbw as Adil Rashid claimed a crucial breakthrough with his first wicket of the series.

Rohit sealed his eighth ODI century on English soil from 84 balls in a 113-run stand with Kohli, as the two legendary Indian batsmen sought a thrilling final chapter in what may prove to be their final international appearances in England.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Rohit Sharma reaches a century in India’s 3rd ODI match against England

Bethell (1-49) bowled Rohit, delivering the crucial breakthrough to reduce India to 260-2, but Kohli's first fifty at Lord's in any format kept the tourists on track.

But Curran's late brilliance derailed the India chase as they were restricted to 360-7 from 50 overs, with England claiming a fifth win from six matches and only their second ODI series victory over India since 2012.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sam Curran takes three wickets in quick succession against India

'Proud' Brook savours series win

England captain Harry Brook:

"I am extremely proud. We fought hard, communicated well like we did in the T20s and have managed to scrape a series win against the world No 1 team.

"We want to set a template with the bat and the way Ben Duckett and Jacob Bethell started with the bat was phenomenal.

"To be no wickets down after 30 overs and not look like they were taking a risk."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player England captain Harry Brook reflects on England’s ODI series victory over India and what it means to the team

Gill rues England's late-innings runs

India captain Shubman Gill:

"I think we were right in the game up until the 45th over [of England's innings]. We gave up too many runs in the last three overs and that's where the game went too far out from us.

"We thought if we had wickets in hand after 40 overs, we would be in the game. After the powerplay, we tried to get the required run rate down."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Shubman Gill was dismissed for 77 as India continue to battle back against England in the 3rd ODI

Root: England developing as ODI side

Player of the Series, Joe Root (249 runs in three games and never dismissed):

"To bounce back from our defeat in the first ODI and beat the No 1 side is the most rewarding thing.

"To back up a brilliant series win in Sri Lanka with this shows we are going in the right direction in a really positive way.

"It is great to see the guys developing and learning."

Sports.title: 'I reached rock bottom' - Antonelli admits shock as title charge accelerates
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli has admitted he could not have imagined being in a dominant position at the top of the Formula 1 world championship 12 months ago when he reached "rock bottom" during his rookie campaign.

Antonelli, 19, won the Belgian Grand Prix for Mercedes on Sunday to move 45 points clear of Lewis Hamilton at the top of the drivers' standings, with 10 of 22 currently scheduled rounds complete.

Having been fast-tracked in by Mercedes boss Toto Wolff to replace Hamilton following the seven-time world champion's decision to join Ferrari, Antonelli endured a chastening spell midway through his 2025 campaign.

The then 18-year-old went on a dismal run during which he finished above ninth just once in 10 grands prix, with one of the low points coming as he was knocked out in Q1 in Belgium last year.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli discusses his Belgian GP win and admits he's in a 'good position' after opening up a 45-point gap in the drivers' standings

Asked after claiming his sixth victory of the season on Sunday whether he could have imagined this scenario a year ago, Antonelli replied: "No, absolutely not.

"Last year here, I probably reached the bottom, so it was a very difficult weekend for me mentally.

"But this year was definitely a lot better. If you had asked me last year at this moment, I probably would have said no."

Antonelli's advantage at the top of the standings could actually be far greater if it were not for a spell of bad luck the Italian has endured in recent weeks.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Antonelli wins the Belgian Grand Prix

He suffered an engine failure when running second to Hamilton in Barcelona, and then suffered a wheel-guard failure that dropped him out of the points at the British Grand Prix when he appeared to be on course to chase Charles Leclerc down for victory.

His pace dominance over his team-mate George Russell, who began the year as the clear title favourite, makes it hard to see how Antonelli can be caught unless Ferrari make major improvements to their inferior power unit in the near future.

Despite his strong position, Antonelli is not dwelling on the increasing likelihood of him becoming by far the youngest driver to become an F1 world champion.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Antonelli joins Sky Sports' Karun Chandhok at the SkyPad to analyse the Italian's pole-setting lap at the Belgian Grand Prix

"I never want to relax too much," Antonelli told Sky Sports F1.

"Of course, it's a great result and good redemption after last year because last year was a very dark moment for me and to get the win is very special.

"But you can never relax because we have seen in the past how the situation can swing so quickly.

"So that's why it's important to really maximise and take every opportunity that is given, and just make the best out of it because you never know what can happen."

Wolff: We're all surprised by Antonelli form

Wolff made the decision to give Antonelli one of the most desirable seats on the grid when several other strong options were available, and there were times during 2025 when the choice came under great scrutiny.

While Wolff says Antonelli's ups and downs during his debut campaign were expected, the Austrian admits the teenager's remarkable consistency in 2026 has "surprised" the whole team.

"We're all surprised", Wolff said. "I think the first season came as expected. Great moments where his talent shined through, and then moments which were very difficult - the long spell of lack of results in the middle of the season, as expected.

"And then after the winter, also as expected, he knew the environment, he knew the pressures, he knew the demands of the team on the technical side, on the marketing side, knowing the tracks that we would go racing.

"But what was not expected is the serenity and structure that he brought into his game. With Kimi, whether the session was good or bad, you wouldn't see a difference in emotions in the debrief.

"It is absolutely transactional. What is the problem? How do we solve it? How do we move on? And that is new. And I think that's why it's almost when he wins, you can't see this absolute excitement that a 19-year-old would almost have."

Wolff highlighted Antonelli's reactions to the reliability issues that cost him in Barcelona and at Silverstone as further examples of his protégé's level-headedness.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Antonelli suffers damage during the British Grand Prix

Wolff added: "And at the same time, when he fails to deliver results, in Barcelona, when we had the car stoppage, or even in Silverstone, he comes back in and he was the one saying to the team, 'this is a mechanical sport, these things can happen'.

"Nineteen-years-old - that is very impressive to see. And I think this mindset and this attitude is probably one of the main drivers that has allowed the talent to shine so early in his career."

Sports.content:
now 18.33 EDT Pau Cubarsí wins young player of the tournament The Barcelona centre-back gets the nod over teammate and clubmate Lamine Yamal, and it’s thoroughly deserved; Spain conceded one goal in the entire tournament. He looks absolutely delighted, too, and well he should. Share

That’s Argentina’s first attempt at goal all night; their xG is now 0.04. Play is stopped while Merino is checked for concussion. Share Updated at 17.55 EDT

39m ago 17.54 EDT 116 min What the hell was that? Williams beats Molina on the left, moves into the area and tries to find Torres with a showboaty flick when a simple low pass would suffice. He makes a total mess of it and knocks the ball out of of a goalkick. If Spain don’t win the World Cup, he’ll regret that for the rest of his natural-born days. Share Updated at 17.58 EDT

40m ago 17.52 EDT 115 min Messi takes a short corner on the right, gets it back and curls a big, dipping cross that briefly startles Simon before landing on the roof of the net. Share Updated at 17.53 EDT

41m ago 17.52 EDT 115 min Ferran Torres is a very good player, not a great one. But he is few minutes away from joining the best club in world football. These are the men who have scored the winning goal in a World Cup final: Angelo Schiavio, Alcides Ghiggia, Helmut Rahn, Gerd Muller, Jorge Burruchaga, Andreas Brehme, Andres Iniesta, Mario Gotze. Share Updated at 18.32 EDT

42m ago 17.51 EDT 114 min: Torres has a goal disallowed. It looked very tight as he ran through from the halfway line to beat Martinez, but the semi-automated technology confirmed the decision straight away. View image in fullscreen Ferran Torres is a fraction offside. Photograph: John Sibley/Reuters Share Updated at 17.59 EDT

44m ago 17.49 EDT 111 min Mac Allister is booked for a foul on somebody or other. Argentina look semi-resigned to their fate. Share

46m ago 17.47 EDT 110 min That was Spain’s 20th attempt at goal, 12 on target. Argentin- ah you know that. Share

47m ago 17.46 EDT 108 min If Argentina win the World Cup from here, they will go down as football’s greatest mentality monsters. Share

48m ago 17.44 EDT Spain go in front 37 seconds after the restart. Pedro Porro’s deep cross is headed back deftly by Nico Williams, and Torres lashes it into the roof the net with his left foot! Share Updated at 18.17 EDT

50m ago 17.43 EDT 106 min The last 15 minutes of the World Cup final are under way. Share Updated at 17.46 EDT

52m ago 17.41 EDT “Once, just once,” says Andy Flintoff, “I’d like to see a top team with non-inverted wingers. Argentina have put five across the width of the penalty box and Yamal and Williams are turning right into them the moment they get the ball.” Share

53m ago 17.40 EDT Half time in extra time: Spain 0-0 Argentina It’s worth repeating that Argentina have not had a single attempt at goal, yet they are 15 minutes away from a penalty competition they will probably win. Spain have had 19 attempts at goal, 11 on target. Share

54m ago 17.39 EDT 105+2 min Torres pushes Tagliafico over off the ball. Spain are starting to lose the head, which is not the way to beat this Argentina team. Share

55m ago 17.38 EDT 105+1 min Three minutes of added time. On the disallowed goal, the foul looked pretty soft but I guess it falls under the umbrella of referee’s call – had it been given on the field, I doubt VAR would have intervened. Share Updated at 17.40 EDT

1h ago 17.35 EDT 105 min There’s some aggro on the touchline, after which Lionel Scaloni is booked. Share

1h ago 17.35 EDT 104 min Since you asked, Andres Iniesta’s winner in the 2010 final came in the 116th minute. Share

1h ago 17.34 EDT 103 min: Chance for Merino! Williams’ inviting, inswinging cross from the left is headed fractionally wide of the far post by Merino. He timed his run superbly but had to stretch to meet the cross and that’s why it went wide rather into the corner. View image in fullscreen Mikel Merino goes so close for Spain! Photograph: Carl Recine/Getty Images Share Updated at 17.40 EDT

1h ago 17.33 EDT 102 min: Argentina substitution Marcos Senesi replaces Julian Alvarez, which means Argentina will be playing 5-3-Messi for the rest of the game. Share

1h ago 17.32 EDT 101 min Yamal shoots miles wide at the end of another patient Spain move. This is going to penalties. Share

1h ago 17.31 EDT 100 min Fair to say these teams have contrasting records in World Cup penalty competitions. Argentina W6 L1

Spain W1 L4 Share

1h ago 17.30 EDT 99 min: Triple substitution for Spain Martin Zubimendi and Eric Garcia replace Rodri and Aymeric Laporte. Share

1h ago 17.29 EDT 97 min: No goal Ah, I missed Merino accidentally standing on Otamendi’s foot. That’s why it was ruled out. Share

1h ago 17.28 EDT 96 min: Disallowed goal for Spain Williams taps a loose ball into the net but the referee has penalised Merino for a challenge just before that. I think he’s given it for a challenge on Otamendi rather than the keeper, but it looks pretty soft. A VAR check is ongoing. View image in fullscreen Nico Williams thinks he’s scored. Photograph: Jewel Samad/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen It’s pulled back for a very, very soft foul on Nicolas Otamendi. Photograph: Carl Recine/Getty Images Share Updated at 17.33 EDT

1h ago 17.25 EDT 93 min Pedri’s flat cross brushes the head of Williams and is pushed away by the diving Martinez. A fairly comfortable save; I think Williams might have been offside anyway. But Martinez is racking up the saves: that’s his 11th. Argentina haven’t even managed a shot off target. Share

1h ago 17.23 EDT 91 min Extra time is under way. No more substitutions. Share Updated at 17.23 EDT

1h ago 17.18 EDT Spain have dominated every facet of the game. They lead too, but only when it comes to men on the field: it’s 11-10 after Enzo Fernandez was sent off after receiving two yellow cards. Argentina have been so ineffective that victory on penalties is surely inevitable. Share

1h ago 17.17 EDT Full time: Spain 0-0 Argentina The World Cup final is heading to extra-time, but first we’ll have a two-hour concert from Blink 182. All the hits. Share Updated at 17.17 EDT

1h ago 17.16 EDT 90+8 min: Good save from Martinez! Yamal curls the free-kick around the wall and Martinez flies to his left to push it round the post! A dramatic save, but one he’d expect to make. View image in fullscreen Emi Martinez saves Argentina again. Photograph: Kai Pfaffenbach/Reuters Share Updated at 17.27 EDT

1h ago 17.15 EDT 90+6 min Paredes, who is also on a yellow, trips Ferran Torres 23 yards from goal. That could have been another red card. I don’t think it quite reached the threshold but it wasn’t far away. Share Updated at 17.15 EDT

1h ago 17.14 EDT 90+5 min Now Messi is claiming that Marc Cucurella covered his mouth while talking to him. That’s quite interesting because he ignored it when Declan Rice did something similar the other day. We haven’t seen a replay but play has resumed so Cucurella has presumably been cleared. Share

1h ago 17.13 EDT 90+5 min After complaining for 60 seconds or so, Enzo Fernandez finally leaves the field. Share

1h ago 17.12 EDT 90+3 min: Enzo Fernandez is sent off! The ball rebounded back upfield after that Martinez save. Fernandez clattered into Cubarsi, who went flying, and was given a second yellow card. The contact wasn’t that bad but it was a stupid challenge from Fernandez and there’s no way this will be overturned. View image in fullscreen Brainless from Enzo Fernandez Photograph: Lars Baron/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Photograph: Kevin C Cox/Getty Images Share Updated at 17.14 EDT

1h ago 17.11 EDT 90+3 min The free-kick eventually leads to a poor low cross from Simeone, too close to Simon. Spain break and Williams whacks a shot from 20 yards that is beaten away by Martinez. And then… Share Updated at 17.14 EDT

1h ago 17.10 EDT 90+2 min Messi runs into Laporte and goes flying. Argentina’s players complain but the referee settles for a free-kick. Share

1h ago 17.09 EDT 90+1 min “One of those World Cup knock-out games when you pray from 80 mins that there won’t be an undeserved late winner,” writes Adam Hirst, “because this match deserves ET and the pain of pens.” Share Updated at 17.09 EDT

1h ago 17.08 EDT 90+1 min There will be four minutes of added Spain possession. Share

1h ago 17.08 EDT 90 min Rodri breaks forward, into space, only to shoot over from 25 yards. Spain have been much the better team – but Emi Martinez still hasn’t had a really difficult save to make. Share

Sports.title: World Cup final: Trump, half-time show and everything but the football – live
Sports.content:
5m ago 18.28 EDT Trump and Infantino booed as they enter field Just to clarify that all three leaders of the host countries – Claudia Sheinbaum, Mark Carney and Donald Trump will present the trophy. Trump and Infantino are roundly booed as they enter the field. Share Updated at 18.28 EDT

13m ago 18.20 EDT The stage is now being set up on the field, where Spain will receive the trophy from media shy duo Donald Trump and Gianni Infantino. Share

20m ago 18.13 EDT Christopher Smith writes in: “Any chance we can get Animal from the Muppets to hand off the trophy instead of the other muppet Trump?” Share

20m ago 18.12 EDT Some differing reactions from the two teams at the final whistle… View image in fullscreen Spain v Argentina at full-time. Photograph: John Sibley/Reuters Share

23m ago 18.09 EDT Carlos Alcaraz is in the stands looking significantly happier than when he won any of his grand slams. And he didn’t look disappointed when he won those ones. Share

25m ago 18.08 EDT Argentina are not taking this well: Molina punched a Spanish sub as he ran on to the field to celebrate. Because how dare someone celebrate winning the World Cup? Share

1h ago 17.25 EDT As things stand, Cape Verde have scored more goals against Argentina than Spain and England combined. Share

1h ago 17.23 EDT The hafltime show lasted just over 27 minutes. So we’ll have seen Animal drumming for almost as long as we’ll watch extra time. I know that’s incredibly strained but I’m killing time until Trump grabs the trophy at the presentation ceremony and runs away laughing. Share

2h ago 17.02 EDT Trump is shown looking quite animated in the executive box. By this point in the NBA finals, he had nodded off to sleep. Share

2h ago 16.58 EDT The news is in: the World Cup final is a sell-out. The New York Jets have sold out this stadium, so I’m not sure that counts as an achievement. Share

2h ago 16.54 EDT Phil Udell writes in: “I’m a big fan of Coldplay’s efforts to be an ethically sound modern stadium band but how does that sit with allying themselves with such a questionable organisation as Fifa, to say nothing of their pal in the White House?” I imagine they’ll point out that the halftime show was to promote Fifa’s charity efforts. But … good point. Nathan North: “If the score is still 0-0 at the end of extra time, instead of the lottery of penalties, I think the only fair thing to do would be to give the World Cup to the winner of the third place match.” Share

2h ago 16.51 EDT Trump wasn’t shown on the video screen at the stadium during the halftime show – Fifa is smart enough not to offer a distraction. We did see Carlos Alcaraz, Serena Williams and Zidane though – none of whom were booed. How could you boo Carlos anyway? Share

2h ago 16.41 EDT Facundo Iglesia is in Buenos Aires for us. Here’s how things are going there: A small screen hanging outside a travel agency in downtown Buenos Aires draws a crowd of hundreds. If the sound is even on, it’s drowned out by the monotone drone of vuvuzelas, the crackle of firecrackers, and the fans chanting: “El que no salta es español” (“Anyone who doesn’t jump is a Spaniard”) and the better-known but less appropriate version, “El que no salta es un inglés” (“Anyone who doesn’t jump is an Englishman”). Thousands across the capital are watching the final this way - people in Albiceleste jerseys wandering the area around the Obelisco, catching glimpses of TVs inside or outside businesses, jumping and shouting as if they were at East Rutherford Stadium in New Jersey. But those scattered pockets of fans carry a well-known risk: spoilers. Broadcast delays across TV channels and radio stations are a running annoyance in Argentina, and a group of supporters reacting to a play will sometimes tip off another group nearby - before the play has even happened for them. A respectful round of applause, for instance - later revealed to be for Lisandro “Licha” Martínez leaving the pitch - rippled down the block a full beat before the screen outside an empanada shop caught up. “It’s annoying - that’s why I’m watching the screen with commentary on my phone,” says Carla Lucía del Pardo, a 31-year-old pastry chef. “That way, I gain five seconds.” For Del Pardo, Argentina is playing “well, but too calm.” “They’re defending the goal, but not really going on the attack,” she added. Share Updated at 16.42 EDT

2h ago 16.32 EDT Reader verdicts on the half-time show Gillian Forrester: “You did not mention that the fabulous Gustavo Dudamel was conducting! He’s moving to the NY Phil this fall (and is Venezuelan, FYI).” Matthew Leung: “I hope that is the only World Cup half-time show I ever have to see in my life. 17 minutes of underwhelming, cringeworthy crap. I am a BTS fan, but this wasn’t really a great ad for them.” Brigid Brennan: “Did I hear some boos for Pele when he appeared on screen? (From Argentinian fans, presumably). It was a choice to have a heavy Brazilian influence in front of a pro Argentinian crowd - Ronaldo, Ronaldinho & Pele.” Philip Reed: “For three decades soccer fandom in the US, both MLS and especially international club, has had a strong undercurrent of, ‘This is the sport that it’s OK to care about and still be somewhat artsy’. It’s also why there’s little overlap of say watching Premier League games at 8am with the “soccer mom” culture of piling the kids in the SUV and remembering to bring the orange slices for halftime. They’re just two different sets of cultural signifiers. Maybe this World Cup will merge the two a bit.” Leo Addor: “The thing was going well until they brought on Ted Lasso and then Bieber. Bieber seemed like a homeless guy who cut up his own clothes and then wandered onto the pitch to play guitar about some weird Christian bullshit (which is basically accurate). “Burna Boy seemed like he was contractually obligated to stay at least 1/2 feet away from Shakira at all times. Their dynamic was weird. “They showed Dua Lipa watching afterwards. She seemed to think that she could’ve done better, and well, she’s right.” Share Updated at 16.34 EDT

2h ago 16.22 EDT I’m not sure how much the players would have enjoyed trying to keep themselves warmed up during that extended break. Maybe Messi, 56, had a nice nap. Maybe there was a unifying theme to that halftime show – probably something to do with football uniting the world – but Bad Bunny it was not. Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl half-time show review – a thrilling ode to Boricua joy Read more Share

2h ago 16.20 EDT Wayne Rooney gives his verdict on the half-time show ... “I like a lot of them artists but I thought it was crap.” Don’t ever change, Wayne. Roy Keane liked Shakira. Share Updated at 16.38 EDT

2h ago 16.17 EDT And so, we go back to the football. Were the professional singers who performed professional? Yes! Were the cute kids who performed cute? Yes! Did anyone ask for this? No! Did this add to the World Cup final? Not really! Will it convert neutral American fans to soccer? No! Would an exciting game without a big interruption in the middle do a better job of that? Yes! What I’m saying is that they should just have shown highlights of England 6-4 France from yesterday instead. Animal was good though. View image in fullscreen The best bit of the halftime show. Photograph: James Lang/IMAGN IMAGES/Reuters Share Updated at 16.18 EDT

2h ago 16.14 EDT A kids choir from Staten Island – who says nothing good comes out of Staten Island – are joined by Kermit and Miss Piggy next. Shakira has such affection for Staten Island that she comes along to join them. And Chris Martin, who is curating this show. This is very wholesome and nice and professionally done. Does the World Cup final need it … probably not? Share

2h ago 16.11 EDT Shakira and Burna Boy are next up. They bring on some cute kids to dance, which – understandably – goes down well with the crowd. Share

2h ago 16.10 EDT Bieber shows his improv skills by adding “World Cup” to the lyrics of his song. They don’t pay him the big bucks for nothing (he’s playing for free, for charity) Share

2h ago 16.09 EDT Alexander Abnos I am running the TV broadcast of this halftime show alongside watching it live at the stadium and, unsurprisingly, this stuff absolutely does not translate live. It took til halfway through Seven Nation Army for me to realize Animal was playing the drums. View image in fullscreen The Muppets at the World Cup final. Obviously. Photograph: James Lang/IMAGN IMAGES/Reuters Share Updated at 16.11 EDT

2h ago 16.08 EDT Here comes Ted Lasso and Coach Beard to introduce …Justin Bieber. Bieber is 32 now, so is unlikely to win a professional football contract. Good voice though! Share

2h ago 16.06 EDT BTS are their usual professional, excellent selves as they belt out Dynamite. They may have played one or two stadium gigs in their time. They get more air time than Madonna, but fewer Brazilian World Cup winners. Share Updated at 16.07 EDT

2h ago 16.05 EDT Animal is on the drums as they play Seven Nation Army. OK, this is now an excellent halftime show. Forget any previous criticism I had of it. In fact, just stop it here. After a quick Viking Row, BTS are on – with no Animal. Share

2h ago 16.04 EDT And we’re on Madonna is on a car driven by Ronaldo (the Brazilian one) and … Ronaldinho. I hope they have travel insurance because that car doesn’t look that roadworthy. They’re driving on to the field now. Ronaldo looks very happy to be there. Share

3h ago 16.02 EDT They’ve rolled out a big tarp at the New York New Jersey Stadium as they prepare the field for the performance. It’s been a great day for tarps at today’s final. Share

3h ago 15.58 EDT Just a reminder that the halftime show will last 25 to 30 minutes. Around 11 minutes for the actual show and the rest of the time to set up the stage and then take it all down. There are worries that the added down time for players could lead to injuries as muscles cool down due to inactivity. On the upside, they’ll get to hear Justin Bieber sing for about 90 seconds. The list of artists includes: Shakira; Burna Boy; BTS; Madonna; Kermit and Miss Piggy; conductor Gustavo Dudamel with musicians from the New York Philharmonic and the Simon Bolivar Symphony Orchestra of Venezuela; dance troupe Ghetto Kids; Emmanuel Kelly; PS 22 Chorus (cute kids from a local school). Share

3h ago 15.56 EDT Alexander Abnos The half-time show approaches, which means uber-warmup man Michael “Let’s Get Ready To Rumble” Buffer is back, and he is yelling very loud. Talk about someone who should be booed Share Updated at 16.39 EDT

3h ago 15.47 EDT Does the World Cup final need a halftime show? The argument for the halftime show seems to be that it’s what new fans want. James Massing of Live Nation, who are helping put on the show, told the BBC that sports events need to change things up because they are “competing with any other live experience - going to the museum, going to the theatre, going to the cinema”. I’m pretty sure no one going to the museum expects a halftime show though, and people are still happy to queue up to see the Mona Lisa without one. I suspect that this is also a push by people who think that US fans will refuse to watch a big event unless it has a halftime show, even though plenty of big sporting events, from the NBA finals to the World Series don’t have halftime shows. I actually think the appeal of soccer to many Americans is that it’s not the NFL, in the same way that many European fans enjoy the NFL because it’s not soccer. And people expect a halftime show at the Super Bowl because it’s the Super Bowl, not because they expect - or want - one at a World Cup final. Added to that, the best Super Bowl halftime shows often provide commentary on the state of America, from Bad Bunny’s hymn to immigrants at this year’s Super Bowl to Beyonce’s black panther tribute in 2016. Somehow, I doubt Gianni and friends are going to allow Shakira to sneak in references to the Iran War today. On the upside, all the artists are performing for free, there will be a kids choir and the show is meant to support Fifa’s education fund. Share

3h ago 15.30 EDT Sam Jones Madrid’s Plaza de Colón, famous for its massive Spanish flag, is absolutely rammed as the match begins. Police are turning people away from the barriers that have been installed around the square, but the mood inside it somewhere between expectant and buoyant. No one wants to hex the game but hopes are high.



“It’s a historic moment and it’s really exciting,” said Katy, 18, who was two years old the last time Spain won the World Cup. “I’m obviously hoping that Spain win and I think it’ll be 3-2 to Spain.” Miguel Hinojal Vicente, 37, had come to Madrid from Toledo as much for the party atmosphere as for the match itself. Unlike Katy, he had vivid memories of Spain’s last World Cup triumph. “Shit, it was just a magical thing,” he said. “But, to tell the truth, I’m more of a Atleti fan than a Spain fan.” His friend Raquel Garcia was a little more enthusiastic - and optimistic. She predicted a 3-0 win for Spain, with two goals in the first half and one in the second. But it was about more than just football for her. “This is about the hopes of a country and it’s about unity,” she said. “Events like these bring people together and they make people happy.” Share

3h ago 15.25 EDT Rusty Shpork gets in touch: “Are any of the online prediction markets taking bets on the exact minute Trump nods off? I’m going with the 27th minute, after he’s exhausted himself rage-bleating on Truth Social during the first commercial break about the large number of “probably illegal” Latinos in the stadium. If Spain win, Trump will probably try to present the trophy to Messi, anyway. Brand recognition, yada yada.” Share

Sports.title: Kane says Tuchel will ‘learn a lot’ from England pressures after exit to Argentina
Sports.content:
Harry Kane has backed Thomas Tuchel to learn from England’s World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentina and believes they must use the forthcoming Nations League campaign to gain experience of playing against the top teams.

Kane was an unused substitute as England sealed third place with an entertaining 6-4 victory against France on Saturday – their best finish at a World Cup on foreign soil. Tuchel, who signed a contract extension before the tournament, has been criticised heavily for his tactics against Argentina when he opted to switch to a back five to try to defend a 1-0 lead.

Kane admitted England had fallen short against Lionel Scaloni’s side but described the environment Tuchel has created since succeeding Gareth Southgate in 2025 as “the best England group I’ve been a part of in terms of togetherness”.

The captain said: “I know there are a lot of questions after the other night. We have to process it as players. I’m sure the manager will. It’s his first major tournament. He’ll learn a lot from the players, the situations, the pressures, the travel.

“There are also a lot of things as players we can learn from the other night. For now it’s just trying to process everything. We had a lot of good things, a lot of tough situations we overcame. The group is incredible, the best England group I’ve been a part of in terms of togetherness. The boss was a big part of creating that as well.

“Fans are going to be angry and we understand it. It’s a major tournament and that’s why you dream so big. When it doesn’t go your way you have to take the criticism. We’re all willing to do that, to dare to reach the biggest goal of all. We know over the next two years until we’re facing that situation again there is always going to be a question mark. It’s something we have to take and use as motivation.”

England missed out on facing regular top-class opposition in the buildup to the World Cup after being relegated from the top Nations League group in 2022 under Southgate. They were promoted in 2024 and will face Spain, Croatia and Czechia, starting with a rematch of the Euro 2024 final against Luis de la Fuente’s side on 26 September at Wembley. After beating France – albeit in a largely meaningless game – Kane thinks England must take the competition seriously if they are to thrive in tournaments.

View image in fullscreen Defeat to an established opponent was a familiar feeling for England. Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty Images

“The last 30 minutes of Argentina is not the team we want to be,” he said. “We spent a lot of time over the last two years talking about that situation, to attack those moments. The bottom line is we lost anyway. It’s easy to go away and talk about it. We need to get better at actually being in those situations. We can train, play the qualifiers … I think the Nations League will be big for us, against Spain and Croatia, big teams.

“Getting used to those big environments and finding our best form against those teams, like we did against France, albeit not in the most competitive match. We have to learn, improve. The coach will have improved from these learnings. I can talk as much as I want but ultimately it’s about showing it next time we’re in that situation.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Kane has been on the losing side in two World Cup semi-finals and two European Championship finals and he believes Tuchel is the man to help England to make the final step.

“The enthusiasm he has, the emotion he brings, the tactical experience he has … it doesn’t mean you’re going to get it right every time. We want to get it right on the biggest occasions and he expects that from himself as well. He’s a fantastic coach. He not only gave the players belief but he gave the country belief that it was our year. That is why it hurts even more than other years because everyone believed we were going all the way.

“Everyone has to process it. He has to process it himself. We’re still in that grieving stage, the emotional stage, and we’ll be in that for the next few weeks. It won’t be until the next camp where you think about what the future holds and what the next target is. We’ll have conversations as captain and manager and with other teammates and staff, to see where we can be better.”

Sports.title: Football Daily | Give it up for Vozinha, Spence and the 2026 World Cup’s cult heroes
Sports.content:
WE CAN BE HEROES

Every World Cup produces cult heroes, icons who make it possible for us to sit back and start misty-eyed recollections by saying: “Do you remember Roger Milla/Saeed Al-Owairan/Keisuke Honda/Paul the Octopus?” Well, the Geopolitics World Cup has not let us down! Here are 10 cult heroes who’ve emerged from this tournament.

Yaya Sithole: a catastrophic start as the South Africa midfielder’s error led to the first goal of the GWC against Mexico, compounded by a second-half red card. Bounced back with a vital display in the win over South Korea, leading his country to the knockout round. Decades from now, people will still be talking about the Yaya Sithole redemption arc. Possibly.

Vozinha: who else? Cape Verde’s players all became cult heroes, but especially the 40-year-old keeper who spent last season in the Portuguese second tier and this summer keeping out Spain as the Blue Sharks went unbeaten in the group stage, then pushed Argentina to extra time in the last 32. Vozinha’s mum: get in line – we’re all in his fan club now.

Djed Spence: a toss-up with Dan “the modern-day header-beast” Burn for England’s cult hero, but let’s give it to the Spurs full-back who transformed from the hapless scourge of Thomas Tuchel’s existence in the group stage to a chin-strapped Cafu in the knockout round. Spence’s slide tackle on Giuliano Simeone (albeit sans chin-strap) will live long in the memory.

View image in fullscreen Djed Spence to the rescue. Photograph: Will Oliver/EPA

Matías Galarza: Paraguay’s most magnificent git was always involved despite rarely trying to play football. Almost every time we saw the midfielder he was moaning, playacting, needling opponents – truly putting the “art” into the dark arts. Also scored against Turkey and later nicked the referee’s watch and strapped it to his own wrist. Timeless ’housery.

Keyne: poor Lamine Yamal, who turned a craggy 19 during the GWC, must be feeling pretty aged considering he’s been usurped by his three-year-old brother. Keyne gurning and giggling in the crowd has delighted fans in Spain and beyond. Considering some of the other people who’ve hogged TV cutaways, the toddler has been a welcome sight.

Iván Barton: Salvadorian referee grabbed the globe’s attention when he sent off Miguel Almirón, bawling at the winger like a mum sending a misbehaving youngster to bed with no dinner. “After review, No 10, Paraguay, covered his mouth! The decision is red card!” No PlayStation either, Miguel!

Eloy Room: move over, Vozinha, and make room for Eloy! Yep, another veteran goalie starred at this GWC as Curaçao bounced back from shipping seven (7) against Germany to hold Ecuador to a 0-0 draw. The 37-year-old Room made 15 saves – a record for a 90-minute World Cup match – to earn the tiny Caribbean island their first ever point.

View image in fullscreen Eloy Room to the rescue. Photograph: Ed Zurga/AP

Danny Murphy: or should it be Bob the cat? The deadpan BBC pundit’s tale of how a family moggy once made a break for freedom inside a Royal Mail van – sparked by Oscar Bobb coming off the bench for Norway – proved so engrossing that viewers demanded, and got, several follow-ups. A purr-fect hydration-break diversion. Honk!

Hossam Hassan: Egypt’s perma-angry, black T-shirted head coach was an intimidating presence – especially paired with his identical twin brother, the team director, Ibrahim Hassan. The pair had a row with Dallas police, led the Pharaohs to the last 16, saw Egypt take a 2-0 lead against Argentina … before the final 15 minutes helped Hossam reach new heights of apoplexy.

Romelu Lukaku: how can Belgium’s record goalscorer be obscure enough for cult-hero status? Well, when you polish off USA USA USA 4-1 and celebrate your 93rd international goal with a Trump dance near the corner flag in the aftermath of Balogungate. Thanks, Big Rom (Bigliest Rom?) – the planet is with you.

View image in fullscreen Romelu Lukaku to the rescue. Photograph: Lindsey Wasson/AP

LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE

Join Rob Smyth from 8pm BST (3pm EST, 5am AEST) for hot updates from Spain 1-1 Argentina (aet; 4-5 on pens) in the GWC final. The animals below agree, though the punters in New York City disagree. Meanwhile Tom Lutz will be in situ for another liveblog mopping up all other business outside the game, which we’re tempted to call Everything But The Goal.

View image in fullscreen Moo Deng, a two-year-old female pygmy hippopotamus, picks Argentina at Khao Kheow Open Zoo in Thailand Photograph: Anusak Laowilas/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

View image in fullscreen Poty the jaguar sides with the holders too at BioParque, in Rio de Janeiro. Photograph: Tita Barros/Reuters

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“This game will help us for sure – even if you can never fully celebrate a bronze medal. It’s the first [men’s World Cup] medal for 60 years, first [at a men’s] World Cup on foreign soil, and I hope the players can be proud of that at some point. We set ourselves the highest dream to chase, and we were very, very ambitious with our dream to make the final in the World Cup. So it’s very, very painful if you miss out, the pain will stay for a while” – England head coach Thomas Tuchel after overseeing a quite preposterous 6-4 win over France in the Third Place Play-off.

View image in fullscreen England with their bronzes. Photograph: Paul Childs/Reuters

double quotation mark May I be one of the 1,057 pedants to point out that it’s little wonder Brazil lost to Poland in the 1970 TPPO (yesterday’s Football Daily) as they would have been resting players for the next day’s final against Italy (which they won 4-1 to claim their third world crown – Pelé, Carlos Alberto and all that). You must have meant the 1974 TPPO. Easy to be fatigued at this stage of the tournament; just ask Harry Kane” – Jonathan Westwood (and 1,056 others).

Sports.title: Fifa gives fraud ‘an open door’ with betting, says Council of Europe chief
Sports.content:
Fifa has been accused of providing an “open door to fraud” and allowing political influence to cast doubt on the integrity of the World Cup in a stinging rebuke by the Council of Europe’s secretary general.

In an open letter published to coincide with Sunday’s final, Alain Berset also called for a new integrity framework to be built before the 2030 tournament, which is mainly being staged in Europe, and warned that Fifa was embroiled in a crisis involving money and power.

Berset referenced the scandal surrounding Fifa’s decision to shelve the suspension of the USA striker Folarin Balogun and made apparent allusions to comments made by the Paraguayan senator Celeste Amarilla about Kylian Mbappé and by the former Spanish prime minister Mariano Rajoy about the France team.

“The Fifa World Cup 2026 has raised question after question,” Berset wrote. “A sanction suspended under pressure, within days, with no reasons given. The authority of referees called into question. Racist abuse of players, some of it from elected officials. Betting on every pass, every card, every corner. The celebration will end tonight. The questions will not.”

It is a significant intervention given Fifa and the Council of Europe signed a memorandum of understanding in 2018, which remains valid. The agreement was struck to strengthen their work together on a number of topics, including “human rights, integrity and good governance in sport”. Open criticism of one partner by another is extremely rare.

Berset took aim at Fifa’s deal with ADI Predictstreet, which became the World Cup’s official prediction market partner in April. “Betting has moved from the result of a match to moments a single player can produce without changing the score,” he said. “A bet is won by making others lose. It is an open door to fraud. And this World Cup has opened the door wider.”

In further reference to the lifting of Balogun’s ban by Fifa, which occurred after a phone call to its president, Gianni Infantino, by his US counterpart, Donald Trump, Berset said: “When the rules bend under pressure, every result is open to doubt.”

View image in fullscreen Gianni Infantino with Donald Trump at the World Cup final reception at Trump Tower on Friday 17 July in New York. Photograph: Ira L Black/Fifa/Getty Images

Infantino has said the decision to revoke Balogun’s ban was taken independently by Fifa’s disciplinary committee “based on the applicable regulations and the specific facts”.

Berset, who is Swiss, proposed a “working dialogue that starts tonight” to begin the “urgent work of strengthening the integrity of sport” before future World Cups. He referenced work by the Council of Europe – which is the continent’s intergovernmental human rights organisation – in creating a binding treaty to keep fans safe three months after the Heysel Stadium disaster in 1985, as well as further legislation set up to tackle doping in athletics and match-fixing.

The letter comes a week and a half after 72 members of the European parliament wrote to the 27 EU-based football associations asking for an investigation into Infantino’s involvement in the Balogun case. It pointed to alleged breaches of political neutrality and suggested Fifa had contravened its own code of ethics.

It does not appear likely that Uefa, European football’s governing body, will formally take the matter further. In June, 50 members of the European parliament wrote to Infantino and the Fifa council requesting an investigation into the awarding of the Fifa peace prize to Trump.

Fifa was contacted for comment.

This past week it was revealed that more that 200 of Fifa’s member associations have formally backed Infantino’s attempt to be re-elected for a fourth term in March.

Sports.title: England 2026 World Cup squad: player-by-player ratings
Sports.content:
Goalkeepers

Jordan Pickford Could he have done better with Enzo Fernández’s equaliser for Argentina? Jude Bellingham certainly thought so. But the man who has made more World Cup finals appearances than any other Englishman made some crucial saves, including a brilliant stop from Nicolas González in the semi-final. 7

Dean Henderson Had to wait until the third-place playoff for some action and ended up conceding four goals despite a strong performance. Will hope to challenge Pickford over next two years. 7

Defenders

Djed Spence Emerged as an unlikely cult hero thanks to some wholehearted performances. He will always be remembered for snubbing Thomas Partey’s handshake and his tackle on Giuliano Simeone against Argentina. 8

Marc Guéhi Somehow wasn’t Thomas Tuchel’s first-choice initially, although that was rectified after the Croatia game. England’s most consistent and reliable defender – the way he handled Erling Haaland was a masterclass. 8

John Stones Arrived painfully short of match fitness and it showed in the opening game against Croatia. Much improved when called upon in the quarter- and semi-finals. A huge asset when he plays. 7

Ezri Konsa A few shaky moments during the group stage but recovered well and filled in capably at right-back when needed. At 28, young enough to be there again in four years. 7

View image in fullscreen Dan Burn’s headed block from this Raúl Jiménez bicycle kick cleared the halfway line. Photograph: Ulises Ruiz/AFP/Getty Images

Dan Burn Showed his limitations against Argentina. But he will always have those two epic appearances off the bench against Mexico and Norway. No one will forget the clearing headers so powerful they ended up in the opposition’s half. 7

Nico O’Reilly Had his strongest game against Norway in the quarter-final when he was at his marauding best. Will be disappointed not to have scored and to have been on the pitch as a substitute when Argentina instigated their semi-final comeback. 6

Reece James Such a good player when fit, which is sadly far too rare. Missed most of the tournament owing to a hamstring injury and England suffered when he went off against Argentina. 6

Trevoh Chalobah The Chelsea player was a surprise choice to replace Tino Livramento, who pulled out injured at the last minute. Managed only six minutes against France in the end. 6

Jarell Quansah Brought in to solve the right-back conundrum against Panama, he was doing well until the rush of blood against Mexico and subsequent red card. Recalled for the France game and had to be replaced. 5

Midfielders

Jude Bellingham Showed his supreme quality when it mattered and could not be more committed to his country’s cause, even if his rocky relationship with Tuchel had to be carefully managed. 9

Elliot Anderson Didn’t allow himself to be distracted by his £116m move to Manchester City and grew as the tournament progressed. Ran his heart out against Norway and Argentina. 8

View image in fullscreen Morgan Rogers (left) crossed for Anthony Gordon to put England ahead against Argentina. Photograph: Julian Finney/FIFA/Getty Images

Morgan Rogers Made the most of his limited minutes in unfamiliar roles. Showed what a good player he is by playing as one of the two central midfielders against Norway before setting up Anthony Gordon from the right wing against Argentina. 8

Declan Rice Clearly affected by the hamstring and back problems that marred the second half of his season with Arsenal, even if his effort – as ever – could not be faulted. Needs a long rest to recharge his batteries but may not get one. 6

Eberechi Eze Could not have the impact he would have wished for in four substitute appearances before starting against France. Did a decent job in central midfield against Panama but was largely on the periphery when given a chance on the left in the quarter-final. 6

Jordan Henderson Spent 12 minutes on the pitch, in a historic appearance against Panama when he became the first England men’s player to appear at seven major international tournaments. But managed to get booked against Mexico as a substitute and break an arm celebrating the win. 5

Forwards

Bukayo Saka Three goals and three assists despite playing through the pain of an achilles injury was a courageous effort from Arsenal’s talisman. It was a huge surprise not to see him come off the bench against Argentina and he showed what England were missing against France. 8

Anthony Gordon A quiet start having been preferred to Rashford before responding magnificently to being dropped. Three assists and a goal against Argentina showed why Barcelona were so keen to sign him. 8

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane’s two goals against the Democratic Republic of the Congo saved England from an early exit. Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPA

Harry Kane Sadly his tournament will be remembered for a largely anonymous display against Argentina rather than rescuing England against the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Will he ever have a better chance to win the World Cup? 8

Marcus Rashford Made a good start to his third World Cup by coming off the bench to score against Croatia, and started against Panama. But wasn’t seen again until England were chasing the game against Argentina in injury time. 6

Ivan Toney Sat on the bench until Lautaro Martínez’s goal in added time of the semi-final. Could not make an impact in the three minutes he was given but did well against France. 6

Ollie Watkins Largely a frustrated spectator despite his heroics in the Euro 2024 semi-final and arriving here in a rich vein of form. A half on the left flank against France and a brief appearance against Panama were scant reward. 6

Noni Madueke Some promising moments but lacked end product in his four starts and had slipped down the pecking order by the semi-final. Needs to be much more clinical at this level. 5

Did not play: James Trafford and Kobbie Mainoo

Sports.title: Fifa to announce record $15bn World Cup revenue, smashing expectations
Sports.content:
Fifa will announce record $15bn (£11.2bn) revenues from this summer’s World Cup, significantly exceeding the targets set before the tournament.

Fifa’s member associations were informed of the boost in income by Gianni Infantino on Saturday. Originally the governing body had projected $11bn in earnings. Sources have indicated that hospitality and ticketing, especially through the steeply priced secondary market, account for a significant amount of the increase. Fifa takes 15% from the buyer and another 15% from the seller on the secondary market.

It is likely that football associations will reap the benefits of Fifa’s expanded World Cup pot, although details are yet to be finalised. The financial situation will come as a boost to Infantino, who will feel it further shores up his position after a controversy-ridden month in the US, Canada and Mexico.

There was widespread fury after Fifa was perceived to have bowed to pressure from Donald Trump in suspending the red card given to Folarin Balogun, the US striker, against Bosnia and Herzegovina in the last 32. Fifa has said the decision was taken independently by its disciplinary committee but that has continued to fester among European FAs in particular. Infantino has nevertheless received more than 200 pledges of support from Fifa’s member associations for his re-election in March. The prospect of extra funds from bumper World Cup revenue is likely to dissuade some FAs from making any discontent public.

Such a bonanza may also increase the chances of the US hosting another edition in the near future. The next World Cup available for bids is the 2038 tournament. At a reception on Friday, Trump confirmed his country’s eagerness for a repeat performance. “You should choose the United States of America again,” he said. “This time we will leave Canada and Mexico out.” The US has also held talks with Fifa about hosting the Club World Cup in 2029.

On Saturday evening, VIP and hospitality packages for Sunday’s final between Spain and Argentina, which was played in New Jersey, were still listed on Fifa’s ticketing portal. Tickets for the “trophy lounge” were retailing at $34,500 per person.

Sports.title: America’s World Cup report card: some As for atmosphere, but F for affordability
Sports.content:
Come rain or smokescreen, Sunday will bring the 2026 World Cup to its bombastic end. The load-bearer of the co-hosting North American trio, the United States held 78 of the tournament’s matches across its 11 host cities. Only two contests remain: the third-place game in Miami, and the big one in East Rutherford, New Jersey.

Before the dust truly settles and focus shifts to the six-nation, three-continent centennial in 2030, how did the United States fare in its second swing at hosting a men’s World Cup?

Stadiums

Depending on what you’re looking for, best in class. Few venues have “charm” in the traditional sense, but these sprawling NFL venues packed in plenty of fans, with many designed to retain sound to harness atmosphere. That said, none seem to have figured out how to adequately keep a concourse congregation flowing, with those corridors hardly expanded to account for so many people in one building. B+

Transport

This was an anticipated drawback of holding this tournament in the US, as the nation rebuilt itself throughout the 20th century with clear priorities for the automobile. Some cities stepped up their public transportation options with ad‑hoc buses; others used those initiatives to further eat into riders’ spending budgets. Hours spent slowly progressing to venues, and even more slowly when leaving, were equally costly. D+

Affordability

Do we even need to explain this one? The expectations for ticket pricing made public in United 26’s bid book were in line with what we’ve come to expect for World Cups, with inflation largely justifying modest increases from tournament to tournament. Instead, the 2026 World Cup became an outlier for event pricing of nearly any kind – the first that most of the world could never afford to attend.

Fifa admitted this was a rare chance to spawn an ATM from the tournament’s rib, and that the ludicrously priced inventory wouldn’t be sustainable for future installments on other continents. An unapologetic slap in the face of USsoccer fans. Once Fifa set this precedent, every other stakeholder in the tournament – transport, food and beverage vendors, merchandisers, parking lot operators, taxis, everyone – followed suit. F

View image in fullscreen Even if you had a ticket to a World Cup match in Philadelphia, the price of parking was no small feat. Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty Images

Hospitality

On the one hand, the displays of community were incredibly touching. No matter how overpriced the lager was, it was common to see traveling fans from all over the world clinking cups before and after the match. Fifa’s legion of volunteers were smiling faces in neon tracksuits, awfully helpful and welcoming at every turn.

On the other hand, not all fans were quite so well accommodated. Referees and team staffers were among those turned away by Trump administration decisions. That precedent also left the general fan from a Trump-banned nation without a chance of getting around policies. The rationale for those rejections was incredibly flimsy, yet Fifa stood beside the man in the White House.

It will be impossible not to wonder how different the support of Côte d’Ivoire, Haiti, Iran and Senegal could have been had the tourist accessibility of the 1994 World Cup been replicated. A for the spirit fostered by those who could make it, but F for the unprecedented barriers set before qualifiers and customers alike.

Atmosphere

The category with the biggest discrepancies between the best-in-class and the rest. Some – Seattle, Philadelphia and Kansas City – cemented an identity of being organic and sustainable soccer cities. The “World Cup village” atmosphere so many fans covet was alive and well, with accessible public watch parties, signage and flags lining streets, and a constant buzz of excitement that the world’s eyes found their neck of the woods. Others, like Boston – the second capital of Scotland – and the Bay Area either embraced their temporary occupants or had plenty of space and opportunities for locals to keep the party going between matchdays.

Others, especially those whose stadiums weren’t in or adjacent to the city center, really struggled to harness the tournament’s potential. It turns out being an hour or two away from the action feels just as invigorating to some as watching a game from their sofa. Texas seemed especially agnostic despite being one of two states with multiple host cities, with dispatches from Dallas and Houston reading equally blase. The roadshow has already packed up, and many in some of these cities will hardly recognize what came through. B-

Sports.title: Spain fans direct sarcastic chants of 'Infantino' at FIFA President after Nico Williams goal controversially disallowed - amid 'rigged' World Cup accusations
Sports.content:
Spain fans directed sarcastic chants at Gianni Infantino after Nico Williams saw a goal chalked off in extra-time for a 'soft' foul on Nicolas Otamendi.

With the score poised at 0-0 in the first-half of extra-time, the Spanish winger thought he'd won it when he slotted a side-footed effort under Emi Martinez.

But as Williams wheeled away to celebrate Slovenian referee Slavko Vincic - taking charge of his first World Cup final - blew his whistle to signal a foul.

He deemed that Mikel Merino had trampled on the foot of Otamendi moments before Williams found the back of the net, causing the ex-Man City defender to collapse dramatically to the floor.

It was a decision which was reviewed but ultimately upheld by VAR, sparking fury in the stands at the 80,000-capacity MetLife Stadium.

The thousands of Spaniards who flocked to New Jersey were heard chanting 'Infantino', not for the first time on the afternoon, as if to accuse the FIFA President of 'rigging' the tournament in Argentina's favour.

Nico Williams was left bemused after seeing a goal in extra-time of the World Cup final disallowed

It came after Mike Merino was deemed to have trampled on the toes of Nicolas Otamendi

Alan Shearer was one of those who criticised the call to disallow what would have been the game's opener. The ex-England striker said on the BBC: 'Was it just the way Mikel Merino went sliding in? That is not a foul for me.

'The only thing I can see is there is a slight touch of the toes on Nicolas Otamendi's toe, but not enough for me to give it as a free-kick.

'Otamendi makes a meal of it and that's what has won them the free-kick.'

The notion of a rigged World Cup is one which has plagued much of this tournament, with fans questioning whether referees have been biased towards Lionel Messi in what is almost certainly his final major tournament.

The South Americans had struggled on their route to the World Cup final, and only narrowly scraped past Cape Verde, Egypt and Switzerland in their early knockout games.

The manner of those victories - in which Egypt had a goal controversially disallowed and the Swiss saw striker Breel Embolo sent off - resulted in huge backlash and speculation that FIFA are conspiring to help Messi and Argentina win the tournament - an accusation the governing body strenuously deny.

After the Argentinians overcame Switzerland 3-1, ex-Man City defender Manuel Akanji fumed: 'Every little thing was called against us' and 'I've never experienced such a one-sided game.' Manager Murat Yakin called the refereeing 'incomprehensible'.

While after the Egypt game in Atlanta, which finished 3-2, the Africans' winger Mostafa Ziko said: 'This tournament has been fixed'. It came before coach Hossam Hassan fumed: 'This match was rigged, and the whole world saw it.'

FIFA's chief refereeing officer Pierluigi Collina responded, stating that 'nobody can question the integrity' of the refereeing and 'unfounded allegations have no place in our sport'.

Argentina's so-called luck, however, ultimately ran out in New Jersey on Sunday night as Spain rallied after the disallowed goal to find a winner.

It came through Ferran Torres in the 106th minute. After a ball was swung in from the right, Nico Williams nodded a header down from the far post, which the Barcelona striker latched on to and fired into the roof of the net to spark jubilant scenes.

The South Americans applied pressure of their own in search of a goal late on and Tottenham Hotspur defender Marcos Senesi almost levelled from close range.

But, in the end, it wasn't to be for Lionel Messi on what could his final appearance on football's biggest stage as Lamine Yamal and his Spanish team-mates held on for a historic victory.

Joe Hart said on the BBC: 'They were never rattled or under pressure. They haven't nibbled once. They played beautiful football the entire time.

'Yamal, at 19 years old, his confidence, the ways that he's doing this. Everyone will be trying to get on his back and hate on him, but he's got a Euros and World Cup. He kept so cool, kept his head, and had those standout moments.'

The match was, however, at times overshadowed by the antics of the Argentinians.

After taunting England's stars in Atlanta on Wednesday, Argentina's behaviour against Spain was dubbed 'embarrassing by pundits' after the final whistle in New Jersey.

Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez saw red in the 90+3-minute for a late challenge on Pau Cabarsi before chaotic scenes were sparked on the pitch when Spain's win was confirmed.

As the Spanish bench descended onto the pitch to celebrate, Argentinian substitute Leandro Paredes took issue with Barcelona midfielder Gavi.

The pair became embroiled in a row, causing Scaloni to intervene, before Paredes appeared to direct two punches at Gavi as he fell to the turf.

And, speaking on the BBC, ex-Man United striker Wayne Rooney was scathing in his criticism of Argentina's behaviour not only on Sunday, but throughout the tournament.

He said: 'It doesn't surprise me. We've seen this from Argentina before. It's just sad, very poor from them. If you lose a game of football, be graceful. It's a reaction to them being outplayed. Enzo Fernandez has got what he deserves it's well.'
